blocks.h: 1. (a) The three principles the LLMC regime is built on

blocks.p: The Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 was adopted on 19 November 1976 and entered into force on 1 December 1986. It rests on three organising ideas.

ol: A right to limit that is, in practice, unbreakable. Article 1 gives it to shipowners, charterers, managers and operators, to salvors, to those for whose acts they answer, and to their insurers. Article 4 removes it only for that person's personal act or omission, committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Because the fault must be personal, negligent navigation by the master does not break it.

The limit is fixed by tonnage, not by fault and not by the size of the loss. Article 6 computes a global amount from gross tonnage, with a higher tranche for loss of life and personal injury than for property; Article 7 deals separately with passenger claims.

One fund per occurrence, distributed rateably. Articles 11 to 13 allow a single limitation fund; claimants are confined to it and rank rateably, and other assets are protected from arrest for those claims.

blocks.h: 2. How LLMC links to the other liability conventions

blocks.p: LLMC is the general, residual regime, and the specialised conventions relate to it in two opposite ways.

ul: Conventions with their own limits stand outside it. The CLC 1992 creates strict, channelled liability on the registered owner for tanker oil pollution, with its own limits, compulsory insurance and direct action. LLMC therefore expressly excepts CLC oil pollution claims at Article 3.

Conventions with no limits of their own borrow LLMC's. The Bunkers Convention 2001 imposes strict liability but sets no limits; its Article 6 preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, in practice LLMC. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 does the same at Article 10(2).
So a bunker spill and a wreck removal limit in the LLMC fund; a tanker cargo spill is dealt with under CLC. States may, however, reserve against LLMC applying to wreck removal.

blocks.h: 3. (b) The liabilities that are subject to limitation

blocks.p: Article 2 lists the limitable claims, whatever the basis of liability may be:

ul: loss of life or personal injury, and loss of or damage to property, occurring on board or in direct connexion with the operation of the ship or with salvage operations, including consequential loss;
loss resulting from delay in the carriage of cargo, passengers or their luggage;
loss resulting from infringement of rights other than contractual rights in direct connexion with those operations;
raising, removal, destruction or rendering harmless of a wrecked or sunken ship and its cargo, subject to reservation;
claims by a person other than the person liable for measures taken to avert or minimise loss.

blocks.h: 4. The claims left outside, and the conduct that breaks the limit

ul: Article 3 excepts claims for salvage and for contribution in general average - a salvor's earned award cannot itself be cut down by the regime;
CLC oil pollution damage and nuclear damage, each having its own regime;
claims by servants of the shipowner or salvor where the law governing the contract of service does not permit limitation;

and under Article 4 the limit falls away on proof of the person's own intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge that such loss would probably result - a burden on the claimant, and very rarely discharged.

blocks.h: 5. (c) The principles of the Salvage Convention 1989

blocks.p: The International Convention on Salvage, 1989 was adopted on 28 April 1989 and entered into force on 14 July 1996, replacing the Brussels Convention of 1910. Its principles are:

ul: salvage is a voluntary service to property in danger, outside any pre-existing duty, and no cure, no pay is the base rule - a reward is earned only by a useful result;

the reward is fixed on the Article 13 criteria - salved value, the skill and efforts of the salvors in preventing or minimising environmental damage, measure of success, nature and degree of danger, time and expenses, risk of liability, promptness, availability of vessels and equipment - and may not exceed the salved value;

Article 14 special compensation corrects the blind spot in the 1910 regime: where the vessel threatened environmental damage and the salvor earned no reward, or a lesser one, the owner pays his expenses plus up to 30% where such damage was minimised or prevented, which a tribunal may raise to 100% of expenses if fair and just;

Article 8 imposes duties both ways - due care and best endeavours to prevent or minimise environmental damage on the salvor, and full co-operation on owner and master. Commercially the regime is worked through Lloyd's Open Form, with SCOPIC as a tariff-rate alternative to assessing Article 14.

blocks.h: 6. Why salvors may limit, and the limit that applies

blocks.p: The rationale is a specific failure of the earlier regime. In The Tojo Maru a salvage company's diver, working in the water and not on board the salvage tug, negligently caused an explosion in the casualty. Under the 1957 Convention a salvor could limit only when operating from a vessel and where the act was done on board or in her navigation or management; the diver's act was neither, so the salvor faced unlimited liability.

LLMC 1976 answered it directly. Article 1 makes salvors persons entitled to limit, and Article 1(3) defines a salvor broadly as any person rendering services in direct connexion with salvage operations - which covers the diver in the water. Because such a salvor may have no ship at all, Article 6(4) supplies a notional figure: his limits are calculated according to a tonnage of 1,500 tons.

That deemed tonnage falls in the lowest band, not exceeding 2,000 gross tonnage. In a State party to the 1996 Protocol as amended by the 2012 amendments, in force 8 June 2015, the applicable limits are 3.02 million SDR for loss of life or personal injury and 1.51 million SDR for property claims. A State bound only by the unamended 1976 Convention applies lower figures, so the instrument in force for that State must be identified before any figure is quoted. India is a party through Part XA of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 - the Act in force at the date of this examination - the Protocol and its amendments being given effect by rules made in 2015 and 2017.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The paper prints 5 + 5 + 6 and the route puts two headings under each limb, so an examiner marking limb by limb can see all three answered without hunting. The commonest way to lose marks here is to write a single essay about limitation of liability in which limb (c) never gets a separate treatment, and the specific figure asked for never appears at all.

blocks.h: Limitation is not insurance, and not liability

blocks.p: These three are constantly confused and the distinction is worth holding firmly. Liability asks whether you must pay. Insurance asks who reimburses you when you do. Limitation asks how much you must pay, whatever the true size of the loss - and LLMC pays nobody. It caps recovery from the shipowner or salvor by reference to tonnage, an arbitrary but predictable measure chosen precisely because it can be known in advance and insured against. That predictability is the commercial point of the whole regime: without it, marine risk could not be written.

blocks.h: The architecture in one idea

blocks.p: There is a general regime and there are specialised ones, and the exam-worthy question is always which applies. If the specialised convention brought its own limits - CLC - it displaces LLMC and LLMC excepts it. If the specialised convention created strict liability but brought no limits - Bunkers, Nairobi - it points back at LLMC. Get that one sentence right and limb (a) is largely answered.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Listing conventions by name without saying how any of them links to LLMC, which is what limb (a) actually asks.
Saying the right to limit is lost by negligence. It is lost only on the person's own intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge - not the master's navigation.
Forgetting that salvage and general average are excepted from limitation altogether, which is the neat counterpoint to limb (c).
Quoting a limit figure without saying which instrument the State is bound by. The unamended 1976 figures are lower.
Treating special compensation under Article 14 as a second reward. It is compensation for expenses, and it exists because no cure, no pay would otherwise pay nothing for preventing pollution.
Omitting the deemed tonnage of 1,500 in Article 6(4), which is the hinge of the last part of limb (c).

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Three main principles' - the examiner has fixed the number. Give three, clearly separated.
'linkage with two other IMO Liability and compensation Conventions' - two, and the linkage must be explained, not merely named.

'specify the current liability limit applicable to them' - a figure is being asked for. An answer that discusses salvors' limitation in principle and never states 3.02 and 1.51 million SDR has not answered the question.
The printed comma splice - 'as established by the IMO, Furthermore, examine' - is on the paper. It joins two demands; answer both.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This is one of the most stable questions on the paper, and it is worth understanding why that can be asserted rather than hoped. The LLMC limits were last raised with effect from 8 June 2015 and the tacit acceptance machinery had not been used again at the date of this paper - and that can be asserted rather than hoped, because an instrument verified unchanged at a later date cannot have been different before it. The Salvage Convention 1989 is unamended. What is not primary is the figure source: MIW holds no licensed copy of the 1996 Protocol consolidated text, so 3.02 and 1.51 million SDR rest on the IMO convention page. India's Part XA implementation rests on practitioner commentary and was not read in the statute; the answer therefore states the Convention position and flags the Indian variation rather than asserting its content. Current note: Part XA sat in the Merchant Shipping Act 1958, which was repealed from 15 March 2026 - see Q5 - so a candidate revising today should confirm the corresponding provision of the Merchant Shipping Act 2025.

questions.understand_first: Limiting liability is not the same as insuring against it, and the two are constantly confused. LLMC does not pay anybody. It caps what a claimant can recover from the shipowner or salvor, whatever the true size of the loss, and it does so by reference to tonnage - a measure that has nothing to do with fault, but which can be known in advance and therefore insured. That predictability is the commercial reason the regime exists. The second idea to hold before reading the limbs is that LLMC is the general regime: where a specialised convention brought its own limits it displaces LLMC, and where it brought none it borrows LLMC's.

retrieval_cards.why: Two headings under each printed limb, so the 5 + 5 + 6 split is visible to the examiner.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the three main principles of the LLMC Convention 1976.
retrieval_cards.answer: A right to limit that is in practice unbreakable, given by Article 1 to shipowners, salvors and their insurers and removed by Article 4 only for the person's own intentional or reckless conduct with knowledge. A limit fixed by tonnage under Article 6, not by fault or by the size of the loss. And a single limitation fund per occurrence under Articles 11 to 13, to which claimants are confined and in which they rank rateably.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner has fixed the number at three, so they must be separated cleanly.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does LLMC relate to CLC 1992 on one hand and the Bunkers Convention on the other?
retrieval_cards.answer: CLC 1992 carries its own limits for tanker oil pollution, so LLMC expressly excepts CLC oil pollution claims at Article 3. The Bunkers Convention 2001 imposes strict liability but sets no limits of its own, and its Article 6 preserves the right to limit under the applicable regime, in practice LLMC. The Nairobi Wreck Removal Convention 2007 does the same at Article 10(2).
retrieval_cards.why: This is the linkage limb (a) asks for - two opposite relationships, not a list of names.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which claims does Article 3 of LLMC except from limitation?
retrieval_cards.answer: Claims for salvage and for contribution in general average; claims for oil pollution damage within the CLC; claims for nuclear damage; and claims by servants of the shipowner or salvor where the law governing the contract of service does not permit limitation.
retrieval_cards.why: The salvage exception is the neat counterpoint to limb (c): a salvor may limit his liabilities, but his earned award cannot itself be limited.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What conduct breaks the right to limit under LLMC, and who must prove it?
retrieval_cards.answer: The person's own personal act or omission committed with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. The burden is on the claimant, and because the fault must be personal to the party seeking to limit, negligent navigation by the master does not break it.
retrieval_cards.why: Article 4. Candidates routinely say negligence breaks limitation; it does not.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is Article 14 special compensation, and how much is it?
retrieval_cards.answer: Where the salved vessel threatened damage to the environment and the salvor earned no reward under Article 13, or a lesser one, the owner pays the salvor's expenses plus up to 30% of them where environmental damage was minimised or prevented, which a tribunal may increase to up to 100% of expenses if it deems that fair and just.
retrieval_cards.why: It exists because no cure, no pay would otherwise pay nothing to a salvor who prevented a major pollution incident but saved no property.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why may a salvor limit, and what is the current limit applicable to him?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because The Tojo Maru exposed a gap - a salvor's diver working in the water and not from the tug could not limit under the 1957 regime. LLMC 1976 brought salvors inside at Article 1, defined a salvor broadly at Article 1(3), and gave a salvor not operating from a ship a deemed tonnage of 1,500 tons at Article 6(4). That falls in the band not exceeding 2,000 GT, so under the 1996 Protocol as amended in 2012 the limits are 3.02 million SDR for loss of life or personal injury and 1.51 million SDR for property claims.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks you to specify the current limit, so the two-step chain from deemed tonnage to figure is where the marks are.

blocks.h: 1. a) What CII is, and where it sits in MARPOL

blocks.p: The Carbon Intensity Indicator is the operational half of the IMO's short-term GHG measure, imposed by MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28, 'Operational carbon intensity'. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above - the threshold of the IMO Data Collection System under regulation 27, on whose fuel data it runs. It must be distinguished from EEXI, a one-off design index applying from 400 gt: EEXI asks what the ship is capable of, CII what she actually did last year.

blocks.h: 2. How attained and required CII are set, and how a ship is rated

ul: The ship calculates an attained annual operational CII - CO2 per unit of transport work over the calendar year. For most cargo ship types this is the AER, CO2 divided by deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed; cruise and ro-pax types use a different metric.

The required annual operational CII is the 2019 reference line for that ship type and size reduced by a factor Z: required CII = reference value x (1 - Z/100). Z is 5% for 2023, 7% for 2024, 9% for 2025 and 11% for 2026, and was extended by resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 to 13.625%, 16.250%, 18.875% and 21.500% for 2027 to 2030.
The attained value is verified annually and the ship rated A to E, C being the required standard, the rating recorded with the Statement of Compliance issued under the DCS.
The factors were set so that, in combination with the rest of Annex VI, shipping reduces CO2 per transport work by at least 40% by 2030 compared with 2008.

blocks.h: 3. What follows from a poor rating

blocks.p: There is no fine and no detention. The consequence is administrative: a ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for one year, must develop a corrective action plan showing how the required index of C or above will be achieved. It is incorporated in SEEMP Part III and agreed before the Statement of Compliance is issued, so a ship that ignores it cannot keep her documentation in order. Incentives to A- and B-rated ships are encouraged.

blocks.h: 4. The commercial impact on the shipping business

blocks.p: The commercial effect far exceeds the regulatory sanction, because the rating is a public, comparable letter grade on an asset:

ul: Chartering. Charterers screen tonnage on rating and some will not fix D or E ships. Because a time charterer controls speed and routing - the very things that set the rating - CII clauses are now standard, notably the BIMCO CII Operations Clause 2022. Who bears a bad rating has become a negotiated term.

Operational control shifts. Owners reserve rights over speed, hull and propeller cleaning and voyage optimisation, so slow steaming becomes contractual - with the machinery consequences of prolonged low-load running that follow.
Finance. Lenders under the Poseidon Principles report portfolio climate alignment, so rating feeds into the cost and availability of debt.
Asset value. A persistent D or E shortens commercial life, depresses second-hand values and brings forward retrofit or scrapping decisions.
Cargo owners. Shippers reporting their own scope 3 emissions demand rating data, so pressure comes from the cargo side as well as the regulatory side.

blocks.h: 5. b) The shortcomings the industry has identified

ul: It rewards capacity, not cargo. The AER denominator is deadweight capacity times distance, not cargo carried, so a ship can improve her rating by sailing further with less on board while absolute emissions rise - a genuine perverse incentive.

Waiting is punished, sailing is not. Idling at anchor adds fuel but no distance. Port congestion and 'sail fast then wait' lie outside the ship's control, and the incentive to keep moving can increase emissions.

Trade patterns are penalised structurally. Short-sea, multi-parcel chemical and product, offshore and ice-class vessels and ships with long port stays are disadvantaged by a metric built around long laden passages, however efficiently run.
Responsibility and control are split. The rating attaches to the ship and the owner's documentation, but a time charterer determines speed, route, waiting and cargo intake.
It is an efficiency ratio used as a climate instrument. Being indexed rather than absolute, improving average CII does not itself guarantee a fall in total emissions.

blocks.h: 6. The remedial measures adopted, and how far the review had got

blocks.p: The regulation anticipated this. Regulation 28.11 requires a review of the CII requirements to be completed by 1 January 2026, covering effectiveness, reinforced corrective action, enforcement, the data collection system, and revision of the Z factor and reference values.

ul: Phase 1 was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025: implementation experience was gathered and analysed and a list of challenges and gaps identified.
Resolution MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025, amended the G3 Guidelines to set the 2027 to 2030 reduction factors, aligning them with the 2023 GHG Strategy's carbon-intensity ambition.
The SEEMP Guidelines were also amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed at future sessions - the door through which a cargo-based metric would have to come.
The industry's own remedies have been contractual - the BIMCO clause - and operational, through just-in-time arrival and virtual arrival schemes aimed at waiting time.

blocks.p: The honest position at this sitting is therefore this. The shortcomings had been formally acknowledged and the review was under way but not complete, with its regulation 28.11 deadline of 1 January 2026 still ahead. What had actually been decided was an extension of the reduction factors to 2030 and an amendment permitting alternative metrics to be developed. The metric itself - the source of most of the criticism - had not been changed, and the remaining stages of the review were still to come.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) carries 10 of the 16 marks and two-thirds of candidates spend all of it on the formula. The four steps force the answer up the ladder from instrument to money, and the commercial half is where the differentiating marks are. Limb (b) is short and is best answered as mechanism then remedy, because a list of complaints without the mechanism that causes them reads as grumbling rather than analysis.

blocks.h: Why an indexed measure behaves this way

blocks.p: Any ratio can be improved by growing the denominator instead of shrinking the numerator. CII's denominator is transport work, and transport work was defined using deadweight capacity because capacity is a known, verifiable number that appears on every certificate, whereas cargo actually carried is commercially sensitive, unevenly recorded and open to manipulation. The choice was made for auditability, and the perverse incentives are the price of that choice. This is worth understanding rather than memorising, because it explains why the fix is hard: a cargo-based metric would need a trustworthy, global, verifiable source of cargo data that does not currently exist.

blocks.h: CII, EEXI, EEDI and the proposed Net-Zero Framework - keeping them apart

ul: EEDI - design index, new ships, regulation 22. What the ship was built to do.
EEXI - design index applied retrospectively to existing ships from 400 gt, regulation 23. A one-off calculation, often satisfied by engine or shaft power limitation.
CII - operational, annual, ships of 5,000 GT and above, regulation 28. What she actually did.

The Net-Zero Framework - the proposed new Chapter 5, a fuel-intensity standard with a pricing mechanism, which at this sitting had been approved and circulated but not adopted. See Q8 of this paper. CII is in force and enforceable; the Net-Zero Framework was not.

blocks.h: What the examiner means by 'remedial measures adopted'

blocks.p: This is the trap in limb (b), and it is a trap about verbs. The industry has asked for a great many things - a cargo-based metric, an exemption for waiting time, relief for short-sea trades. Almost none of that had been adopted. What had been adopted by this sitting was narrower and more procedural: the reduction factors were extended to 2030 by MEPC.400(83), Phase 1 of the review was completed, and the SEEMP Guidelines were amended so that alternative metrics could be developed later. Writing the wish-list as though it were the outcome is the commonest way to lose limb (b), and it is also simply inaccurate.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Calling CII a cap on emissions or an emissions trading scheme. It is neither.
Saying a D or E rating attracts a fine or detention. The consequence is a corrective action plan in SEEMP Part III.
Saying 'CII is the AER'. AER is the metric for most cargo ships; cruise and ro-pax use a different one.
Quoting a reduction factor without its year - the figure changes annually and a bare percentage is unmarkable.
Answering limb (b) with what the industry has asked for rather than what was actually adopted.
Confusing the 5,000 GT CII threshold with the 400 gt EEXI threshold.
Treating the Net-Zero Framework as an existing obligation. At this sitting it was a circulated draft.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'As adopted in MARPOL' - the examiner wants the regulation, not a general essay on carbon intensity.
'Commercial impact in shipping business' is half the limb by weight. An answer that stops at the regulation has answered half of limb (a).
'Shortcomings ... and remedial measures adopted' - two demands in a 6-mark limb. Do not spend it all on complaints.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Your ship is rated E. What actually happens?
Who controls the things that set the rating - you or the charterer?
How can a ship improve her CII while burning more fuel?
What is the difference between EEXI and CII?
Which resolution set the reduction factors beyond 2026?
Does CII apply to a 4,000 GT ship?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Three numbers and three letters. Numbers: 5,000 GT for CII against 400 gt for EEXI; the 2019 reference line; and the Z ladder 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023 to 2026, extended to 13.625, 16.250, 18.875, 21.500 for 2027 to 2030. Letters: A to E, C is the pass, and D three times or E once triggers the corrective action plan. Then the one-line causal chain for limb (b): capacity not cargo, so ballast helps and waiting hurts.

blocks.p: This question was flagged in the corpus as a MEDIUM currency risk, and the review confirms the flag was justified - but also that the decisive events fell on the right side of the line. Resolution MEPC.400(83) was adopted on 11 April 2025 and Phase 1 of the review was completed at MEPC 83, which sat from 7 to 11 April 2025; both are therefore correctly stated here as accomplished, four months before this examination. What could not be brought back from the February 2026 relative is its account of Phase 2 of the review, which opened on 1 January 2026 - five months after this paper was sat. At this sitting the regulation 28.11 deadline of 1 January 2026 was still in the future, and the answer says so rather than describing a process that had not begun.

questions.understand_first: CII is not a cap on emissions and not a trading scheme. It is an efficiency ratio - carbon per unit of transport work - turned into a public letter grade, and almost everything interesting about it follows from those two facts. Because it is a ratio, it can be improved by increasing the denominator rather than reducing emissions, which is where the shortcomings come from. Because it is a public grade attached to an asset, its real force is commercial rather than regulatory: the regulation itself imposes no fine, but a charterer, a bank and a buyer all read the letter. Keep those two ideas separate and both limbs of the question answer themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the CII question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What CII is and where it sits in MARPOL. 2 How attained and required CII are set and how a ship is rated. 3 What follows from a poor rating. 4 The commercial impact. 5 The shortcomings. 6 The remedial measures adopted and how far the review had got.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are the 10-mark limb and climb from regulation to money; steps 5 and 6 are the 6-mark limb, mechanism then remedy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Under which regulation does CII bite, to which ships, and how does that differ from EEXI?
retrieval_cards.answer: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 28, operational carbon intensity, applying to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above - the same threshold as the IMO Data Collection System under regulation 27, whose fuel data it uses. EEXI is a design index under regulation 23 applying from 400 gt as a one-off calculation. EEXI is what the ship is capable of; CII is what she actually did.
retrieval_cards.why: Two thresholds and two characters. Mixing 5,000 and 400 is the commonest factual slip in this topic.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is the required annual operational CII calculated, and what are the reduction factors?
retrieval_cards.answer: Required CII equals the 2019 reference line for that ship type and size multiplied by (1 - Z/100). Z is 5% for 2023, 7% for 2024, 9% for 2025 and 11% for 2026, and was extended by resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 to 13.625%, 16.250%, 18.875% and 21.500% for 2027 to 2030.
retrieval_cards.why: A bare percentage without its year is unmarkable, and the post-2026 figures come from a specific resolution adopted before this sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a ship that is rated D or E?
retrieval_cards.answer: There is no fine and no detention. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or E for a single year, must develop a corrective action plan showing how a rating of C or above will be achieved. It is incorporated in SEEMP Part III and must be agreed before the Statement of Compliance is issued.
retrieval_cards.why: The sanction is documentary rather than penal, and that is precisely why the commercial consequences matter more than the regulatory ones.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can a ship improve her CII rating while emitting more CO2?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the AER denominator is deadweight capacity multiplied by distance sailed, not cargo actually carried. Sailing further, or sailing in ballast, increases the denominator and improves the rating even though absolute emissions rise. Conversely, waiting at anchor burns fuel while adding no distance and worsens the rating.
retrieval_cards.why: This single mechanism explains most of the criticism in limb (b), and stating the mechanism is worth more than listing the complaints.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What remedial measures had actually been adopted by this sitting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Phase 1 of the regulation 28.11 review was completed at MEPC 83 in April 2025; resolution MEPC.400(83) of 11 April 2025 extended the reduction factors to 2030; and the SEEMP Guidelines were amended to allow other CII metrics to be developed at future sessions. The review itself was required to be completed by 1 January 2026 and was not yet complete, and the metric that causes most of the criticism was unchanged.
retrieval_cards.why: Adopted is not the same as proposed. The industry's wish-list - a cargo-based metric, relief for waiting time - had not been adopted.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the split between owner and time charterer matter to CII?
retrieval_cards.answer: The rating attaches to the ship and appears on the owner's documentation, but a time charterer determines speed, route, waiting time and cargo intake - the very variables that set the rating. That mismatch between responsibility and control is why CII clauses such as the BIMCO CII Operations Clause 2022 became standard, allocating the risk of a poor rating as a negotiated term.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the clearest example of a regulatory measure changing commercial contracts, which is what limb (a) is really asking about.

blocks.h: 1. a) What FSA is, and who it is for

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is set out in MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2, 'Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment (FSA) for use in the IMO rule-making process', of 9 April 2018. The title states its purpose: a structured, auditable methodology by which the Organization decides whether, and how, to regulate a hazard, balancing safety benefit against cost. It is not a shipboard risk assessment or a permit-to-work system. The question is therefore how a proportionate rule for this cargo was, and was still being, arrived at.

blocks.h: 2. Step 1 - identifying the hazards of this cargo

ul: Thermal runaway - an exothermic internal reaction that becomes self-sustaining and generates its own oxidant, so it cannot be smothered and continues without external air;
propagation cell to cell and module to module, and thence vehicle to vehicle in a close stow;
initiators - internal cell defects, mechanical damage in handling or lashing, over-charge, a high state of charge on shipment, and charging on board;
vent gas - flammable and toxic, able to accumulate in an enclosed vehicle space and produce a gas explosion rather than a simple fire;
re-ignition hours or days after apparent extinction, defeating a normal fire-out judgement;

mis-declaration and concealment - cells as cargo may be undeclared or wrongly classified, and a battery electric vehicle is not a labelled package at all, so the energy is invisible to the stowage plan.

blocks.h: 3. Step 2 - assessing the risk on a ro-ro deck

blocks.p: Risk is frequency times consequence, estimated from casualty returns, incident and near-miss data, cell testing and fire modelling - with the Rev.2 requirement that the reliability, uncertainty and validity of that data be assessed and reported rather than assumed.

ul: Frequency is low per vehicle but rising with fleet electrification, and exposure is concentrated - one deck may hold thousands of units;

consequence escalates because a ro-ro space is a large undivided volume, vehicles stowed centimetres apart, with no cargo-hold fire divisions and with ramps and ventilation trunks carrying heat and smoke between decks;
on a ro-pax the dominant risk is to life; on a pure car and truck carrier it is total loss of the ship, and a series of well-known casualties supplied the evidence;
manual firefighting on a loaded deck is near impossible, so the model must assume that fixed systems and boundaries are what will actually be available.

blocks.h: 4. Steps 3 and 4 - risk control options and whether they pay

blocks.p: Risk control options are generated and grouped, then tested by cost-benefit assessment using indices such as the cost of averting a fatality, so a measure is recommended only where the safety gain justifies the cost across the world fleet:

ul: detection - earlier, better located, individually identifiable so the seat of fire is known, with combined smoke and heat sensing;
suppression - drencher and water-based systems of adequate coverage and capacity, aligned with detection sections so that the right section operates;
containment - insulated boundaries, ventilation shut-down and control of openings;
operational and design - state-of-charge limits on shipment, segregation and dedicated stowage, restrictions on charging at sea, video monitoring, crew procedures;
options are ranked, and those effective but disproportionately costly are rejected transparently - which is why the outcome is a specific set of measures rather than everything technically possible.

blocks.h: 5. Step 5 - what the recommendations had become by this sitting

blocks.p: The risk-based work on ro-ro fire safety - notably the EMSA FIRESAFE I and FIRESAFE II studies of fire dynamics, system performance and operational factors - entered the regulatory system in stages, and it is important to state precisely how far it had got:

ul: MSC.1/Circ.1615, Interim Guidelines for Minimizing the Incidence and Consequences of Fires in Ro-Ro Spaces and Special Category Spaces, carried key outcomes into guidance while the mandatory work continued. At this sitting this was the operative IMO instrument on the subject;

resolution MSC.550(108), amending SOLAS chapter II-2 regulations 7 and 20, and resolution MSC.555(108), amending FSS Code chapters 7 and 9, had been adopted at MSC 108 in May 2024 - but they were not yet in force. Their entry into force was 1 January 2026, some five months after this examination;

when they did bite they would require individually identifiable fixed detection with combined smoke and heat detectors, detection aligned with deluge sections, detection on weather decks used for vehicles, an effective video monitoring system with at least seven days of replay at a continuously manned control station, and A-60 boundaries on passenger ships carrying more than 36 passengers;
they would apply to ships constructed on or after 1 January 2026, existing ships in scope complying not later than the first survey on or after 1 January 2028;
further amendments aimed specifically at new energy vehicles were still in development.

blocks.p: So the honest conclusion at this date is that FSA had done its work and been acted on - the amendments were adopted, dated and known - but the mandatory regime was prospective. What actually governed the ship on the day was SOLAS II-2 as it then stood, the IMDG Code, and the interim guidelines, which is precisely why limb (b) matters so much at this sitting.

blocks.h: 6. b) Measures by stakeholder

ul: IMO - bring the adopted amendments into force on time, complete the new-energy-vehicle amendments, keep IMDG provisions current and maintain the interim guidance meanwhile;
flag State and class - issue guidance ahead of the compliance dates, and prepare to approve and survey the amended detection, suppression and boundary arrangements;
shipper, manufacturer and packer - correct IMDG classification, packing and marking, state-of-charge control, testing and quality control, and no offering of damaged, defective or recalled batteries;
port and terminal - screen and refuse visibly damaged vehicles, check declared state of charge, separate electric vehicles in marshalling areas, and inform the ship promptly;

ship operator - a written stowage and segregation policy, limits on charging on board, training in lithium fire behaviour, vehicle-deck drills, thermal imaging, and a response plan that assumes re-ignition. Where the fixed systems are not yet those the new amendments will require, this is where the gap is actually closed;

ship's staff - verify cargo against the declaration, maintain detection and drencher readiness, patrol during and after loading, and fight fire by early activation of fixed systems and boundary cooling rather than by entering a loaded deck;
insurers and industry bodies - loss-prevention guidance, incident and near-miss data sharing, and premium signals rewarding compliant stowage - the same data that feeds the next FSA.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The 10-mark limb is a method question, and method questions are marked on whether the method is visible. Naming the five steps and then walking this cargo through them is what separates a top answer from a general essay about battery fires. Step 5 is where most candidates stop short: an FSA that produces no recommendation has not been applied, so ending with what the recommendations actually became - and how far they had got - is what closes the loop.

blocks.h: Why FSA exists at all

blocks.p: Before FSA, IMO regulation was largely reactive - a casualty happened, and a rule followed. FSA was introduced to allow the Organization to act proactively and proportionately, on evidence rather than on the emotional weight of the most recent disaster, and to be able to say publicly why a proposed rule was or was not worth its cost. That is why the Guidelines insist on auditability, traceability and the explicit reporting of uncertainty: an FSA is as much an accountability document as a technical one.

blocks.h: The lithium hazard in engineering terms

blocks.p: Thermal runaway begins when a cell's internal temperature passes the point at which exothermic decomposition of the electrolyte and cathode outpaces heat loss. The decomposition liberates oxygen from the cathode material, which is why the reaction sustains itself without air and why smothering agents - CO2, a foam blanket, an inert atmosphere - do not stop it. Cooling is the only lever the ship holds, and it works by removing heat from cells that have not yet reached onset temperature, so its real objective is to stop propagation to neighbouring vehicles rather than to extinguish the cell already in runaway. That is also why re-ignition is normal rather than surprising: cells that were merely heated may still cross the threshold hours later.

blocks.h: Vehicles, containers and packages are three different regulatory problems

ul: Cells and batteries as cargo - dangerous goods under the IMDG Code, class 9, with UN numbers 3480 and 3481 for lithium-ion and 3090 and 3091 for lithium-metal, subject to packing, marking, documentation and segregation.
Batteries in or with equipment - the same UN family but different provisions, and often carried under exceptions.

A battery electric vehicle - carried as a vehicle, not as a declared dangerous goods package. This is the regulatory gap: the ship may know exactly how many tonnes of declared class 9 she has, and have no idea how much stored energy is sitting on the vehicle decks.

blocks.h: Adopted, in force, and applicable are three different things

blocks.p: This question is a good place to practise a distinction that Q7 of this paper examines in the abstract. Resolutions MSC.550(108) and MSC.555(108) were adopted in May 2024. They entered into force on 1 January 2026. And even then they applied only to ships constructed on or after that date, with existing ships in scope reaching compliance by the first survey on or after 1 January 2028. At this August 2025 sitting the first of those three stages had been passed and the second had not. A candidate who wrote that the new detection and video-monitoring requirements applied to his ship would have been wrong by five months and, for an existing ship, by nearly three years.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Treating FSA as a shipboard risk assessment. It is a tool for IMO rule-making.
Naming the five steps and never applying them to lithium batteries - or applying them and never naming them. The marks need both.
Saying the fire can be smothered or that CO2 will deal with it. Runaway generates its own oxidant; cooling and boundary protection are the levers.
Declaring the fire out. Re-ignition hours later is normal and the plan must assume it.
Stating that the SOLAS II-2 and FSS Code amendments applied at this sitting. They had been adopted but were not yet in force.
Answering limb (b) as a list of things the ship should do, when the question says stakeholders - the chain runs from the cell manufacturer to the insurer.
Forgetting that a battery electric vehicle is not a declared dangerous goods package.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Application of formal safety assessment' - the demand is application, not description. A description of the methodology alone answers half the limb.
'in vehicles and containers and in RORO ships' - three carriage situations, and they are regulated differently. Cover the distinction.
'measures to be taken by stakeholders' in limb (b) - plural and deliberately wide. Group the answer by party.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Five steps, in order and by name: HAZARD - RISK - OPTIONS - COST BENEFIT - RECOMMENDATION. Then hang this cargo on them: runaway and vent gas; close stow and no divisions; detect, drench, contain, restrict; cost per averted fatality; and the actual instruments - Circ.1615 guidance now, MSC.550(108) and MSC.555(108) from 1 January 2026. For limb (b), walk the chain: maker - shipper - terminal - operator - ship - flag and class - insurer - IMO.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This question was recorded in the corpus as temporally stable and at low risk. That was not correct, and the error is stated here rather than quietly repaired. The donor answer for this family closes on resolutions MSC.550(108) and MSC.555(108) as amendments already in force - true from 1 January 2026, and false at this sitting by five months. A question whose answer turns on an in-force date falling between two sittings in the same family is not stable, whatever the printed stem looks like. It was caught by the assembled-answer sweep rather than by the flag, which is a useful demonstration that the sweep is not a formality.

On sourcing: MIW holds no licensed copy of SOLAS or the FSS Code, so the content of the two resolutions rests on a class-society regulatory notice rather than on the amended text. That limitation bears less weight here than at the later sittings, because this answer states their content as what was coming rather than as what applied. No single published IMO Formal Safety Assessment study dedicated to lithium batteries in ro-ro carriage was located, so the answer explains how the method applies to this cargo and identifies FIRESAFE and the resulting amendments as the risk-based work actually done, rather than asserting that such a submission exists. Not a shipboard risk assessment. questions.understand_first: Two things have to be held apart in this question. The first is that FSA is not something the ship does - it is the method by which IMO decides whether a rule is worth making, so the question is really 'how did, and how will, the regulator arrive at a proportionate rule for this cargo?'. The second is that a lithium battery fire is not an ordinary fire: thermal runaway generates its own oxidant, so it cannot be smothered, and the only lever the ship holds is cooling to stop it spreading. Those two ideas shape the whole answer - the method gives the structure, and the physics explains why the risk control options are the ones they are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why can a lithium-ion battery fire not be smothered?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because in thermal runaway the exothermic decomposition of the electrolyte and cathode liberates oxygen from the cathode material, so the reaction sustains itself without external air. CO2, foam blankets and inert atmospheres therefore do not stop it. Cooling is the only lever, and its purpose is to keep neighbouring cells below onset temperature and stop propagation rather than to extinguish the cell already in runaway.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains both why the fixed systems are water-based and why re-ignition hours later is normal rather than a failure of firefighting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the regulatory obligations differ between batteries shipped as cargo and an electric car on a vehicle deck?
retrieval_cards.answer: Cells and batteries shipped as cargo are dangerous goods under the IMDG Code, class 9 - UN 3480 and 3481 for lithium-ion, 3090 and 3091 for lithium-metal - with packing, marking, documentation and segregation requirements. A battery electric vehicle is carried as a vehicle, not as a declared dangerous goods package, so its stored energy does not appear on the dangerous goods manifest at all.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the regulatory gap that drives the whole hazard: the ship can know her declared class 9 tonnage exactly and still not know how much energy is on the vehicle decks.

retrieval_cards.why: Quote these as what was coming, not as what applied - the distinction is the highest-value fact in the question at this sitting.

blocks.h: 1. A) What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: STCW refuses to treat competence as something that time served automatically confers. It replaces experience with demonstrated competence, and then addresses the conditions - fitness, rest, teamwork and company responsibility - under which competence can actually be exercised. The instrument is the STCW Convention and Code, 1978, as amended, most significantly by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force from 1 January 2012.

blocks.h: 2. Competence-based standards

ul: The Part A tables of competence specify, for every function and level, the competence required, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency behind it, the methods for demonstrating it and the criteria for evaluating it - so assessment is against a published standard, not an examiner's impression.
Part A is mandatory; Part B is guidance - a distinction worth stating explicitly.

The Manila amendments added mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level - where engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management enter the Convention. It is the explicit recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a team.
Regulation I/6 governs training and assessment, and regulation I/8 requires a quality standards system, so the training system itself is audited rather than assumed.
Regulation I/11 requires periodic revalidation, and chapter VI mandatory safety familiarisation and basic training before a seafarer is assigned duties.

blocks.h: 3. Fitness for duty - the physical human being

ul: Regulation VIII/1 requires each Administration, for the purpose of preventing fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods for watchkeeping personnel and for those with designated safety, security and pollution-prevention duties in accordance with section A-VIII/1, and to require that watch systems are arranged so that efficiency is not impaired by fatigue.

The Manila-amended A-VIII/1 minimum rest is 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.

Authorised exceptions are tightly conditioned: weekly rest may not fall below 70 hours in any 7-day period, exceptions from the 77-hour norm may not run for more than two consecutive weeks, and daily rest may then be divided into no more than three periods.
The Manila amendments also introduced alcohol limits for masters, officers and other seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards, and regulation VIII/2 with section A-VIII/2 governs watchkeeping arrangements and principles.

blocks.h: 4. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: Regulation I/14 makes the company responsible for ensuring that seafarers hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their duties and with the ship's arrangements, and that documentation is maintained - so the human element is not left as an individual's problem. Administrations operate quality standards systems and are subject to independent evaluation and reporting to IMO.

blocks.h: 5. B) The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The guidance is MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', of 24 January 2019, approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee and finalized by the HTW Sub-Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory - the binding rest-hour requirements remain in STCW chapter VIII and in MLC 2006. The Guidelines are arranged in six modules, each addressed to a different party:

ul: Module 1 - Fatigue: what it is and its causes, grouped as sleep and rest, the biological clock and circadian rhythm, health and stress, environmental factors such as noise, vibration and motion, sleep disorders and operational factors. It defines sleep debt as insufficient accumulated sleep over multiple consecutive 24-hour periods.
Module 2 - Fatigue and the Company: assessing, mitigating and managing fatigue risk in the safety management system, in manning decisions and in scheduling.

Module 3 - Fatigue and the Seafarer: practical guidance for the master, officers and ratings on sleep quality, diet and the limits of countermeasures - notably that caffeine is not a substitute for sleep.
Module 4 - Fatigue Awareness and Training.
Module 5 - Fatigue and Ship Design: mitigation designed in - accommodation location, noise, vibration, lighting and habitability.
Module 6 - Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities: how regulators and inspectors should approach it.

blocks.h: 6. How the guidance and the rules fit together

blocks.p: The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are set by a prescriptive formula in STCW chapter VIII, and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested: managers must allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and - in the Guidelines' own words - rest means rest, not the substitution of a different form of work. The same theme runs through MLC 2006 Regulations 2.3, 2.4 and 2.7. A management-level engineer should therefore treat recorded compliance as the floor, and a rest-hour record that is always exactly compliant as a warning rather than a reassurance.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Two printed limbs of 8 marks each, so split the answer evenly and head each limb clearly. Limb A rewards structure - competence tables, fitness for duty, company responsibility - and limb B rewards naming the actual circular. A candidate who writes generally about tiredness for the second limb without producing MSC.1/Circ.1598 and its module structure will lose most of eight marks, because 'the IMO guidance' is a specific document.

blocks.h: The organising idea for limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on three fronts, and saying so gives the limb a spine: can they do it (competence standards, assessed against published criteria), are they fit to do it now (fitness for duty - rest, medical, alcohol), and who is responsible for making that possible (regulation I/14, the company). The Manila amendments strengthened all three and added the fourth dimension the older Convention lacked - can they work as a team, through mandatory leadership and teamworking training.

blocks.h: The numbers you must get right

blocks.p: 10 hours in any 24, and 77 hours in any 7 days. Divided into no more than two periods, one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rest periods. Exceptions may not go below 70 hours in any 7 days and may not run more than two consecutive weeks. Learn 10, 77, 2, 6, 14, 70 - and be careful, because 70 and 77 are both real figures doing different jobs: 77 is the norm, 70 is the floor under an authorised exception. Quoting 70 as the normal requirement is the classic error, and it is exactly the trap that a pre-2010 copy of the Code will lead you into.

blocks.h: The wrong-edition trap, stated plainly

blocks.p: This is worth a paragraph of its own because it caught this project. A freely available IMO circular copy of section A-VIII/1 - STCW.6/Circ.1 - reproduces the 1995 Code: five paragraphs, 70 hours weekly, and no 14-hour interval provision at all. It looks entirely authoritative, it is on an official domain, and it is superseded. A candidate who revises from it will write 70 where 77 is required and will omit the 14-hour rule altogether. The lesson generalises: for any instrument that has been amended, the question to ask of a source is not 'is this official?' but 'which edition is this?'

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Answering limb B without naming MSC.1/Circ.1598 and the circular it replaced, MSC/Circ.1014.
Treating the fatigue Guidelines as mandatory. They are recommendatory; the binding requirements are STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006.
Quoting 70 hours as the normal weekly rest. 77 is the norm; 70 is the minimum where an exception has been authorised.
Confusing Part A with Part B - Part A is mandatory, Part B is guidance.
Writing about fatigue only, and never addressing competence, which is the larger half of limb A.
Forgetting regulation I/14 - the company's responsibility - which is what turns the human element from an individual failing into a management obligation.
Describing the STCW comprehensive review as though it had produced amendments in force. It had not.

blocks.p: The operative regime is STCW 1978 as amended, with the Manila amendments in force since 1 January 2012 and MSC.1/Circ.1598 since January 2019 - both long settled before this sitting, so nothing here needed re-anchoring from the later relatives of this question. A comprehensive review of the STCW Convention and Code has been under way through the HTW Sub-Committee with completion targeted around 2027, one of the acknowledged gaps being the treatment of hours of rest. Nothing had been adopted at the date of this paper. So write the Manila regime as the operative one and mention the review only as work in progress; do not present any reviewed text as though it were in force.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (A) Human element in STCW. The instrument is STCW 1978 as amended, above all by the Manila amendments of 2010, in force 1 January 2012. It replaces time served with demonstrated competence, then secures the conditions in which competence can be exercised. Competence: the Part A tables give, for each function and level, the competence, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency, the methods of demonstrating and the criteria for evaluating - and Part A is mandatory while Part B is guidance. Manila added mandatory leadership and teamworking at operational level and leadership and managerial skill at management level, bringing engine-room and bridge resource management into the Convention. reg I/6 training and assessment, I/8 quality standards, I/11 revalidation, chapter VI familiarisation before duties. Fitness for duty: reg VIII/1 requires Administrations, to prevent fatigue, to establish and enforce rest periods per section A-VIII/1 - 10 hours in any 24 and 77 hours in any 7 days, in no more than two periods one of at least 6 hours, with no more than 14 hours between consecutive rests. Authorised exceptions may not fall below 70 hours weekly, may not run beyond two consecutive weeks, and allow no more than three daily periods. Manila also added alcohol limits; reg I/9 sets medical standards and reg VIII/2 watchkeeping arrangements. Responsibility: reg I/14 puts valid certification, familiarisation and documentation on the company; Administrations run quality standards subject to independent evaluation. (B) Fatigue guidance. MSC.1/Circ.1598, 'Guidelines on fatigue', 24 January 2019, approved at MSC 100, superseding MSC/Circ.1014 of 2001. It is recommendatory; the binding rest hours stay in STCW chapter VIII and MLC 2006. Six modules: 1 Fatigue and its causes, defining sleep debt; 2 the Company; 3 the Seafarer; 4 Awareness and Training; 5 Ship Design; 6 the Administration and Port State Authorities. How they fit: hours of rest are a prescriptive formula, and compliance is not the same as being rested - allow for circadian rhythm and sleep debt, and treat an always-exactly-compliant record as a warning.

questions.understand_first: The phrase human element is not a polite word for human error. In STCW it means the whole set of conditions that decide whether a competent person actually performs competently on the day - whether the standard he was assessed against was published and objective, whether he has slept, whether he is medically fit, whether he can work as part of a team, and whether his company has made any of that possible. That is why limb A cannot be answered with rest hours alone: rest is one of four fronts. And it is why limb B is a separate document - the mandatory rule sets a floor for hours, while the Guidelines address the thing the floor cannot reach, which is whether the person is actually rested.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the minimum hours of rest under the Manila-amended section A-VIII/1.
retrieval_cards.answer: Not less than 10 hours in any 24-hour period and 77 hours in any 7-day period. The daily rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive periods of rest shall not exceed 14 hours.
retrieval_cards.why: The 14-hour interval is the provision most often omitted, and its absence from a source is the quickest way to tell that the source is pre-Manila.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is the weekly minimum rest 70 hours or 77 hours?
retrieval_cards.answer: 77 hours in any 7-day period is the norm. 70 hours is the floor that applies only where an exception has been authorised, and such an exception may not run for more than two consecutive weeks. Both figures are real; they do different jobs.
retrieval_cards.why: A widely available official IMO circular copy of A-VIII/1 is the pre-Manila 1995 text and gives 70 as the weekly figure. It is official and superseded - always check the edition.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which circular is the IMO guidance on fatigue, and what did it replace?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, dated 24 January 2019 and approved at the 100th session of the Maritime Safety Committee. It supersedes MSC/Circ.1014 on Guidance on fatigue mitigation and management, approved at MSC 74 in 2001. It is recommendatory, not mandatory.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb B says 'the IMO guidance' - a specific document. Naming it and its predecessor is most of the eight marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the six modules of MSC.1/Circ.1598.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Fatigue - what it is and its causes. 2 Fatigue and the Company. 3 Fatigue and the Seafarer. 4 Fatigue Awareness and Training. 5 Fatigue and Ship Design. 6 Fatigue, the Administration and Port State Authorities.
retrieval_cards.why: Each module is addressed to a different party, which is the structural point: fatigue is managed by the company, the individual, the designer and the regulator, not only by the watchkeeper.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the Manila amendments add to STCW on the human element?
retrieval_cards.answer: Mandatory training in leadership and teamworking at operational level and in leadership and managerial skill at management level - bringing engine-room and bridge resource management, situational awareness and workload management into the Convention; revised and tightened rest-hour requirements in section A-VIII/1 including the 14-hour interval rule; and alcohol limits for masters, officers and seafarers with designated safety, security and environmental duties.
retrieval_cards.why: The teamworking addition is the recognition that technically competent individuals still fail as a crew, which is the analytical heart of limb A.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your engineer's rest-hour record is exactly compliant every single week. Is that reassuring?
retrieval_cards.answer: No - it is a warning. The Guidelines are explicit that hours of rest are a prescriptive formula and that complying with the formula is not the same as being rested; circadian rhythm and sleep debt determine whether rest is restorative. A record that is always exactly at the limit suggests the limit is driving the record rather than the work.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the management-level judgement the question is really testing, and it is what separates a Class I answer from a recitation of numbers.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does STCW regulation I/14 require of the company?
retrieval_cards.answer: That seafarers assigned to its ships hold valid certificates, are familiarised with their specific duties and with the ship's arrangements, installations, equipment and procedures before being assigned duties, and that documentation and data are maintained. It places the human element on the company rather than leaving it as an individual's problem.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb A is incomplete without the responsibility front, and I/14 is the provision that supplies it.

blocks.h: 1. What the Act means by an unseaworthy ship

blocks.p: The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 gives no definition of unseaworthiness in a definitions section. The description sits inside section 334 itself, which treats a ship as unseaworthy when the following are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service:

ul: the materials of which she is made and her construction;
the qualifications of the master;
the number, description and qualifications of the crew, including officers;
the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast;
the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery.

blocks.p: Two features carry the marks. The test is relative - fitness for the proposed voyage or service - so a ship adequate for a sheltered coastal run may be unseaworthy for an ocean passage. And it is far wider than material condition: an undermanned ship, one whose officers hold the wrong certificates, or a mechanically perfect ship with badly stowed cargo is unseaworthy under the Act.

blocks.h: 2. The offence, and the defences the Act allows

ul: s.334(1) - every person who sends or attempts to send an Indian ship to sea from any port in India in such an unseaworthy state that the life of any person is likely to be thereby endangered is guilty of an offence, unless he proves he used all reasonable means to insure her being sent to sea in a seaworthy state, or that sending her to sea in that state was, in the circumstances, reasonable and justifiable.
s.334(2) - a master who knowingly takes such a ship to sea commits the offence, with only the second defence available to him.
s.334(3) permits a person charged to give evidence in his own defence; s.334(4) provides that no prosecution shall be instituted except by, or with the consent of, the Central Government.

blocks.p: Liability is therefore not automatic. The threshold is danger to life, the burden of the defence lies on the accused, and the standard demanded is reasonable means rather than a guarantee of result.

blocks.h: 3. What an unsafe ship is, and the power to detain her

blocks.p: Section 336 is directed at a different problem - stopping the ship rather than punishing anybody. An unsafe ship is one which, by reason of the defective condition of her hull, equipment or machinery, or by reason of overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of the service for which she is intended. The procedure is staged:

ol: the Central Government, having reason to believe on complaint or otherwise that she is unsafe, may order her provisionally detained for the purpose of survey;
a written statement of the grounds must be served forthwith on the master;
the matter is referred to the court of survey for the port, or a competent person is appointed to survey the ship and report;
on that report she is either released or finally detained.

blocks.h: 4. The real difference between the two

ul: Unseaworthy is a state; unsafe is the trigger for a power. Section 334 describes a condition and attaches criminal liability to sending a ship to sea in it. Section 336 describes a condition that entitles the Government to stop her.
One looks backwards, the other forwards. The offence punishes a decision already taken; detention prevents the voyage from happening at all.
Unseaworthiness is the wider concept - it expressly takes in crew numbers and qualifications and the stowage of cargo and ballast. The unsafe-ship definition lists a narrower set of causes.
The thresholds differ - life likely to be endangered under s.334; unfitness to proceed without serious danger to human life under s.336.
In practice, a ship unsafe within s.336 will invariably be unseaworthy within s.334, but a ship may be unseaworthy - one certificated engineer short - without being unsafe.

blocks.h: 5. The owner's obligation to the crew

blocks.p: Section 335 converts seaworthiness from a matter between owner and cargo into a duty owed to the people on board. In every contract of service, express or implied, between the owner of an Indian ship and the master or any seaman, and in every contract of apprenticeship, there is implied - notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary - an obligation that the owner, the master and every agent charged with the loading of the ship, or preparing her for sea, or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure the seaworthiness of the ship for the voyage at the time when the voyage commences, and shall keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage.

Three consequences follow. The duty is non-excludable - a term in the crew agreement waiving it is void. It is a due diligence standard, not a warranty of result. And it is continuing throughout the voyage rather than being discharged at departure. It also binds people other than the registered owner: the loading agent is named in the section.

blocks.h: 6. How the obligation is policed, and the statute in force at this sitting

blocks.p: Section 335(2) allows the Central Government, on the owner's request or otherwise, to arrange a survey of the hull, equipment or machinery. In practice the duty is policed through the wider system - class and flag State statutory survey and certification, ISM auditing, and port State control under SOLAS chapter I regulation 19 - with the section 336 detention power as the last resort.

One point of currency should be stated rather than assumed, and it is unusually pointed at this sitting. The Merchant Shipping Act 1958 was the operative law on the examination date. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received the assent of the President on 18 August 2025 - the same month as this paper - but assent is not commencement: it was brought into force only on 15 March 2026, and it is section 324(1) of that Act which repeals the 1958 Act. The answer is therefore correctly and necessarily given on the 1958 Act.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem asks three questions and prints no limbs, so the examiner has no printed structure to mark against and will mark against the three questions actually asked. Answering them in the order asked, with the middle one made explicitly comparative, is what makes the script easy to mark. The comparison in step 4 is the highest-value paragraph in the answer and the one most often missing: candidates define both terms and then never say how they differ, which is literally what was asked.

blocks.h: Why the Act splits the idea in two

blocks.p: A criminal offence needs fault, a trial and proof beyond reasonable doubt, and it operates after the event - which is no use at all to the crew of a ship that is about to sail. An administrative detention power needs only a reasonable belief and can act within hours. The 1958 Act therefore does both: section 334 attaches consequences to a decision, and section 336 supplies the fast preventive lever, with the survey and the right to be told the grounds as the safeguards against its misuse. Seeing that the two sections exist to solve different problems is the whole of the distinction.

blocks.h: Seaworthiness has three different legal lives - keep them apart

ul: Statutory and criminal - MSA 1958 s.334, which is this question. A state of the ship, punishable, with a due-diligence defence.
Contractual, owed to the crew - MSA 1958 s.335. Implied, non-excludable, and continuing through the voyage.

Insurance and carriage - a warranty or a duty of due diligence depending on whether the policy is a voyage or a time policy and on the contract of carriage. Under Indian law that is the Marine Insurance Act 1963, not the English Act of 1906, and a breach affects recovery rather than attracting a penalty.

blocks.p: The examiner asks about the first two. Answering about the third is the commonest way to lose this question.

blocks.h: Assent is not commencement - and this sitting proves it

blocks.p: This paper happens to sit almost exactly on the seam. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 received assent on 18 August 2025, in the very month of this examination, and a candidate who had read a newspaper that week might well have thought the new Act was the law. It was not. An Indian Act ordinarily comes into force on a date the Central Government appoints by notification in the Official Gazette, and here that notification, S.O. 1244(E), appointed 15 March 2026. Between assent and commencement the old Act governs in full. That distinction - passed, assented, commenced - is exactly the same three-stage problem that Q7 and Q8 of this paper examine for international conventions, and it is worth revising the three together.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing seaworthiness in general engineering terms without quoting the section 334 formula.
Leaving crew numbers, certification and stowage out of the definition - they are expressly inside it.
Treating unseaworthy and unsafe as interchangeable, or saying the difference is only one of degree.
Saying the owner guarantees seaworthiness. The duty is to use all reasonable means.
Forgetting that the section 335 duty continues during the voyage.
Answering under the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 or the doctrine of stages.
Answering under the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, which had not commenced and was not the law at this sitting.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Within the meaning of the Merchant Shipping Act (MSA), 1958, as amended' - the examiner is asking for the statutory meaning, and a general definition cannot reach the top band.
'What according to you is the difference' invites an opinion, but the marks are for the legal difference, not a preference.
'Obligations of owners to crew' - section 335 also binds the master and the loading agent, so an answer confined to the registered owner is incomplete.
The printed words 'with respect seaworthiness' are incomplete on the paper. Read them as 'with respect to seaworthiness' and answer the obvious demand; do not waste time on the typography.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: The three sections are consecutive and in logical order: 334 the state, 335 the duty, 336 the power. Inside 334 the definition runs from the fabric of the ship outward to the people and the cargo: materials, construction, master, crew, cargo and ballast, hull, equipment, boilers and machinery - fit in every respect for the proposed voyage. Two phrases are worth memorising word for word: 'fit in every respect for the proposed voyage or service' and 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary'.

MSA 1958 s.335 - implied obligation of the owner to the crew; s.335(2) survey.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, jurisdiction and currency

blocks.p: The statutory position at this sitting is not in doubt: the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 was in force throughout August 2025 and remained so until 15 March 2026. The one thing the source copy does not record is the exact day in August on which the paper was sat, so it cannot be said whether it fell before or after the 2025 Act received assent on 18 August. That does not affect the answer, because assent does not bring an Act into force. The text of sections 334 to 336 was read for QP2602 Q5 in a reproduction of the Act rather than a current official consolidated print, so any later amendment to those sections is unconfirmed; section 334 was cross-checked against a second independent reproduction and agreed. Current note: a candidate revising today must know that these three sections are no longer live law. MIW has not yet mapped the 2025 Act section by section against them, so this guide states the repeal without asserting which provisions replace them.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Unseaworthy - s.334. The Act gives no separate definition; the description sits in the section. A ship is unseaworthy when her materials, construction, the qualifications of the master, the number, description and qualifications of the crew including officers, the weight, description and stowage of the cargo and ballast, and the condition of her hull and equipment, boilers and machinery are not such as to render her in every respect fit for the proposed voyage or service. It is an offence to send or attempt to send an Indian ship to sea from an Indian port in such a state that life is likely to be endangered, with a defence of having used all reasonable means or that it was reasonable and justifiable; a master who knowingly takes her to sea commits the offence with only the second defence. Prosecution requires Central Government consent. Unsafe - s.336. A ship which by reason of defective hull, equipment or machinery, or overloading or improper loading, is unfit to proceed to sea without serious danger to human life, having regard to the nature of her intended service. She may be provisionally detained for survey, with written grounds served forthwith on the master, then finally detained or released after report by a court of survey or an appointed surveyor. Difference. Unseaworthy is a state attracting criminal liability and a duty; unsafe is the trigger for a preventive power. Unseaworthiness is wider and takes in crew and stowage; unsafe lists its causes and demands serious danger to life. Every unsafe ship is unseaworthy; not every unseaworthy ship is unsafe. Owner to crew - s.335. An obligation implied into every contract of service and of apprenticeship, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, that the owner, the master and every agent charged with loading, preparing or sending her to sea shall use all reasonable means to ensure seaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage and to keep her in a seaworthy state during the voyage. The Central Government may arrange a survey under s.335(2). Statute on the day. The 1958 Act governed. The Merchant Shipping Act 2025 was assented on 18 August 2025 but commenced only on 15 March 2026.

questions.understand_first: These are two different legal tools, not two words for the same idea. Unseaworthy describes a state of the ship and is the trigger for a criminal offence and for a duty owed to the crew - it asks who is to blame. Unsafe is the trigger for an administrative power: it lets the Government stop the ship before anyone is hurt - it asks whether this ship sails today. Note also that seaworthiness here is far wider than hull and machinery: an undermanned or badly stowed ship is unseaworthy under the Act even if she is mechanically perfect.
