blocks.h: 1. a) What a general average act is

blocks.p: The statement in the question is correct, and the features are not a matter of opinion: they are drawn from the definition itself. Rule A of the York-Antwerp Rules provides that there is a general average act 'when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure'.

Note first how the Rules apply. They are not law: they take effect by incorporation into the contract of carriage - the bill of lading or charterparty - and the Rule of Interpretation then makes them apply 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. In India the concept is also recognised in the Marine Insurance Act 1963.

blocks.h: 2. The essential features

blocks.p: Every phrase of Rule A is doing work, and each yields one essential feature:

ol: Extraordinary. The sacrifice or expenditure must be outside the ordinary performance of the contract of carriage. Fuel burned on a normal passage, or wear on machinery in ordinary service, is not extraordinary however costly.

Intentional and voluntary. The loss must be deliberately incurred. Cargo washed overboard by a sea is accidental and lies where it falls; cargo jettisoned by decision is a sacrifice. This is the single feature that most sharply separates general from particular average.
Reasonable. Reinforced by the Rule Paramount, which overrides everything else: 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred.'
Peril. There must be real danger - not necessarily immediate, but genuine and substantial, and more than the ordinary risk of the sea.

Common safety and common adventure. The act must be for the benefit of the whole adventure, not one interest alone, and there must be more than one interest at risk. A ship in ballast with no cargo on board has no common adventure and can have no general average.
Preservation of property. The purpose must be to preserve the property from that peril. Success matters: there must be something saved to contribute.

blocks.h: 3. The lettered rules that qualify the definition

ul: Rule C - only losses which are the direct consequence of the general average act are allowed. It expressly excludes demurrage, loss of market, loss caused by delay and any indirect loss whatsoever, and excludes environmental damage and the consequences of escaping pollutants.

Rule D - rights to contribution are not affected even though the event was due to the fault of one of the parties, without prejudice to any remedies or defences in respect of that fault. So the adjustment proceeds first, and blame is fought separately.
Rule E - the onus of proof is on the party claiming, who must give notice in writing to the average adjuster and supply particulars, generally within twelve months.

blocks.h: 4. How the loss is shared, and what general average is not

blocks.p: Under Rule A.2 the sacrifice is borne by the different contributing interests - ship, cargo and freight at risk - rateably in proportion to their values at the termination of the adventure. The adjustment is prepared by an average adjuster, and security is taken before cargo is released, normally an average bond from the receiver and an average guarantee from the cargo underwriter.

Two distinctions complete the picture. General average is not particular average: particular average is accidental damage, falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. And general average is not insurance: it is a rule of contribution between the parties to the adventure, which predates marine insurance entirely, though the contribution is in practice recoverable under the policy.

blocks.h: 5. b) The refloating scenario - the rule that governs it

blocks.p: This situation is dealt with expressly, and by a rule written for exactly these facts. Rule VII, 'Damage to Machinery and Boilers', provides:

'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.'

blocks.h: 6. Applying it - when the damage is allowed, and when it is not

blocks.p: Yes, the burnt bearings can be allowed in general average - provided four things are shown.

ol: The ship was ashore. She was aground, so the first condition is met on the facts given.

She was in a position of peril. This must be established, not assumed. A vessel lying safely aground on soft mud in fine weather, in no danger and awaiting the tide, is not in peril; one working on a hard bottom, or exposed to weather, tide or the risk of breaking her back, is. This is the condition on which the claim will actually turn.

The machinery was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety. Running the engine ahead and astern to shake her off is precisely that - a deliberate act directed at the safety of the whole adventure, not a routine manoeuvre.

The damage arose at the risk of such damage. The master must have accepted the risk of damaging the engine as the price of refloating. Working an engine hard, astern and ahead, against a grounded hull is known to overload the bearings, and it is that knowing acceptance that makes the loss a sacrifice rather than an accident.

blocks.p: The damage then satisfies Rule A as well: it is extraordinary (not ordinary service), intentional (the engine was deliberately worked in a way likely to damage it), reasonable if refloating was a sensible response, and directed at the common safety. It is also the direct consequence of the act, as Rule C requires. Under Rule D it makes no difference to the right of contribution that the grounding may have been somebody's fault.

The converse must be stated, because it is the trap. Rule VII closes with an absolute prohibition: where the ship is afloat, damage from working the propelling machinery is 'in no circumstances' allowed. So if she had already come off and the bearings burnt while manoeuvring clear, or if she were merely touching and not in peril, the same physical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo. The engine damage is identical; the legal answer is opposite; and what decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) is a 'discuss the statement' question, and the highest-scoring way to discuss it is to show that the essential features are not a list somebody invented but the clauses of the Rule A definition read one at a time. That converts a memory answer into an analytical one. Limb (b) is worth the same 8 marks and is decided by a single rule, so the answer must quote Rule VII, apply its four conditions to the facts, and then state the converse. An answer that says 'yes, it is a sacrifice' without naming the rule or testing peril has taken about half the marks available.

blocks.h: Why general average exists at all

blocks.p: It is far older than marine insurance and older than most maritime law - the principle is found in the Rhodian sea law and passed through Roman law into every modern maritime system. The problem it solves is one of incentives at the worst possible moment. If a master must jettison cargo to save the ship, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, then whoever owned that particular cargo would bear everything while the rest of the adventure was saved at his expense. Nobody would consent, and the master's decision would be contested at the moment when hesitation is most dangerous. Making the loss a shared loss removes the conflict: every interest knows that a sacrifice made for the common safety will be contributed to by all. Seen that way, general average is a rule about decision-making under peril, not really a rule about money.

blocks.h: Sacrifice versus accident - the line that decides everything

blocks.p: Almost every general average problem in an examination is a disguised question about whether the loss was chosen. Cargo swept overboard by a sea is an accident; cargo jettisoned is a sacrifice. An engine that fails on passage is an accident; an engine deliberately worked to destruction to refloat the ship is a sacrifice. Water damage from a leak is an accident; water damage from firefighting is a sacrifice. Rule VII is simply that same line drawn for one specific case - and the drafters drew it so firmly that they added an absolute prohibition for the afloat case, because otherwise every hard manoeuvre would generate a claim.

blocks.h: The four conditions of Rule VII, and which one is really in issue

blocks.p: Ashore; in a position of peril; an actual intention to float her for the common safety; at the risk of such damage. In practice the first and third are usually obvious on the facts and the fourth follows from them. The condition that is actually litigated is peril. A ship aground is not automatically in peril - the question is whether she was in real danger, having regard to the bottom, the weather, the tide, her condition and the exposure of the position. That is why a careful answer says the claim 'turns on establishing peril' rather than simply asserting it, and why the master's log, weather records and any surveyor's evidence matter so much afterwards.

blocks.h: Which version of the Rules applies

blocks.p: The York-Antwerp Rules are contractual, not statutory. They apply because the bill of lading or charterparty says they do, which is why the Rule of Interpretation has to declare that they operate 'to the exclusion of any law and practice inconsistent therewith'. The consequence is that the version in force between the parties may be the 1994, 2004 or 2016 text, depending on what the contract incorporates. On this question it does not matter: Rule VII is materially identical in all three. On other questions it can matter a great deal, so the habit of asking which version is incorporated is worth forming.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Listing the features without tying them to Rule A, which is where they come from.
Omitting the requirement of a common adventure - with no cargo on board there is nothing to contribute and no general average.
Forgetting the Rule Paramount. Even a textbook sacrifice is disallowed if unreasonably made.
Answering limb (b) 'yes' without naming Rule VII or testing whether the ship was in peril.
Missing the afloat prohibition, which is the other half of the rule and the source of the marks for a complete answer.
Saying the owner's fault in grounding the ship defeats the claim. Rule D says it does not, without prejudice to separate remedies.
Confusing general average with particular average, or treating general average as a form of insurance rather than of contribution.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'General average is based on certain essential features' - the word essential invites a definitional answer. Give the features as conditions, each of which must be satisfied.
'Discuss the statement' - agreement plus explanation. Do not merely define general average.
'Give justification to your answer' in limb (b) - the justification is the marks. A bare yes or no scores almost nothing.

The facts say 'ahead and astern directions ... to shake the vessel loose'. That wording is doing deliberate work: it establishes both the intention to refloat and the acceptance of risk, so quote it back.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Same damage, but she had just come afloat. Does your answer change?
She is aground on soft mud in fine weather with no danger. Is there general average?
The grounding was the master's navigational error. Does that defeat the claim?
Who prepares the adjustment, and what security is taken before cargo is released?
The ship is in ballast with no cargo. Can there be general average?
Which version of the York-Antwerp Rules applies to your ship, and how do you know?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: For limb (a), hold the six features in the order the definition gives them: EXTRAORDINARY - INTENTIONAL - REASONABLE - PERIL - COMMON - PRESERVING. Then three lettered rules as qualifiers: C direct only, D fault does not matter, E you must prove it. For limb (b), hold Rule VII as four conditions and one prohibition: ashore, in peril, intending to refloat, accepting the risk - but never when afloat.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: This is the most securely sourced question on the paper and the only one researched from scratch. Every proposition in the answer is carried by the text of the York-Antwerp Rules 2016, read in the Comite Maritime International publication - the Rule of Interpretation, the Rule Paramount, Rules A to E and Rule VII, all quoted from the rule text itself. Rule VII was separately confirmed to be materially identical in the 1994 and 2004 versions, which is the point that matters given that the Rules apply by contractual incorporation. Nothing here is time-sensitive: the Rules were unchanged between this sitting and today, and general average is among the most stable doctrines in maritime law.

Two limitations are recorded honestly. First, the section number of the Indian Marine Insurance Act 1963 defining a general average loss was not verified and is deliberately not asserted anywhere - the Act is named, the section is not. Second, no decided case on machinery damage in refloating was read; the answer rests on the rule text, which on this point is unusually explicit and self-contained, and on the analysis of which condition is in practice contested.

quick_revision.recall_15s: (a) Rule A: 'There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.' The essential features are the clauses of that sentence: extraordinary - outside the ordinary performance of the contract; intentional and voluntary - deliberately incurred, which is what separates a sacrifice from an accident; reasonable - reinforced by the Rule Paramount, 'In no case shall there be any allowance for sacrifice or expenditure unless reasonably made or incurred'; peril - real and substantial danger, more than the ordinary risk of the sea; common safety and a common adventure - for the whole adventure and not one interest, so with no cargo on board there is no general average; and preservation of property, so there must be something saved to contribute. Qualifiers: Rule C, only the direct consequence is allowed, and demurrage, loss of market, delay and any indirect loss are excluded; Rule D, the right to contribute is unaffected by the fault of a party, without prejudice to separate remedies; Rule E, the onus of proof is on the claimant, with notice to the average adjuster. Contribution is rateable on the values of ship, cargo and freight at the end of the adventure, adjusted by an average adjuster, with an average bond and average guarantee taken before cargo is released. It is not particular average, which is accidental and lies where it falls, and it is not insurance - it is contribution. The Rules apply by contractual incorporation, not as law. (b) Yes - under Rule VII. 'Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.' Four conditions: she was ashore; she must be shown to have been in peril - the condition that is actually contested; the engine was worked with an actual intention to refloat for the common safety, which working ahead and astern to shake her loose plainly is; and the damage arose at the risk of such damage, the master accepting that risk. The burnt bearings are then an extraordinary, intentional, reasonable sacrifice and the direct consequence of the act. But if she had been afloat, the identical damage would be particular average and the owner's own loss.

questions.understand_first: General average is not insurance and not liability - it is a rule of contribution, and it is one of the oldest ideas in maritime law. The problem it solves is a problem of incentives at the worst moment: if the master must sacrifice one interest to save the whole adventure, and the loss lay entirely where it fell, the owner of that interest would be ruined for everyone else's benefit and would fight the decision. Making the loss shared removes the conflict. Everything in limb (a) follows from that purpose - the sacrifice must be deliberate (or there was no decision to protect), for the common safety (or there is nothing to share), and reasonable (or the decision does not deserve protection). And limb (b) is simply that same test applied to an engine: damage suffered because the master chose to risk the machinery to save the ship is a sacrifice; damage suffered in the ordinary course is not.

retrieval_cards.answer: 1 What a general average act is - the Rule A definition. 2 The essential features drawn from it. 3 The qualifying lettered rules C, D and E. 4 How the loss is shared, and what general average is not. 5 The refloating scenario and Rule VII. 6 Applying Rule VII to the facts, with the converse.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Rule A definition of a general average act.
retrieval_cards.answer: There is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure.
retrieval_cards.why: The essential features are the clauses of this sentence. Quote it and the features write themselves.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the essential difference between general average and particular average?
retrieval_cards.answer: General average loss is intentionally and reasonably incurred for the common safety of the whole adventure, and is shared rateably by all the contributing interests. Particular average is accidental damage which falls on the interest that suffers it and is not shared. The dividing line is whether the loss was chosen.
retrieval_cards.why: Almost every general average problem is a disguised question about whether the loss was deliberate.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Quote Rule VII of the York-Antwerp Rules.
retrieval_cards.answer: Damage caused to any machinery and boilers of a ship which is ashore and in a position of peril, in endeavouring to refloat, shall be allowed in general average when shown to have arisen from an actual intention to float the ship for the common safety at the risk of such damage; but where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average.
retrieval_cards.why: It decides limb (b) outright. The second half - the absolute prohibition when afloat - is the part candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A grounded vessel's main engine bearings burn out while working ahead and astern to refloat her. Is the damage general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, under Rule VII, provided four things are shown: that she was ashore; that she was in a position of peril; that the machinery was worked with an actual intention to float her for the common safety; and that the damage arose at the risk of such damage. Working ahead and astern to shake her loose establishes the intention and the acceptance of risk. Peril is the condition that must actually be proved.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asks for justification, so the marks are in applying the four conditions rather than in the yes.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Would the answer change if the ship had already been afloat when the bearings burnt?
retrieval_cards.answer: Yes, completely. Rule VII provides that where a ship is afloat no loss or damage caused by working the propelling machinery and boilers shall in any circumstances be allowed as general average. The identical damage would be particular average - the owner's own loss, recoverable if at all under the hull policy and not shared with cargo.
retrieval_cards.why: Same physical damage, opposite legal answer. What decides it is the ship's condition and the master's purpose at the moment the engine was worked.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The grounding was caused by the master's negligence. Does that defeat the general average claim?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule D provides that rights to contribution in general average shall not be affected though the event which gave rise to the sacrifice may have been due to the fault of one of the parties to the common maritime adventure, but without prejudice to any remedies or defences open against or to that party in respect of that fault. The adjustment proceeds; blame is dealt with separately.
retrieval_cards.why: It keeps the adjustment moving. Cargo interests can still sue the owner for the fault - they simply cannot use it to refuse to contribute.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Your ship is in ballast with no cargo on board and you sacrifice equipment to save her. Is there general average?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Rule A requires the act to be for the common safety and for the purpose of preserving property involved in a common maritime adventure. With no cargo there is only one interest at risk, no common adventure and nothing to contribute, so the loss falls entirely on the owner.
retrieval_cards.why: The word common in the definition is a condition, not decoration, and this is the quickest way to test whether it has been understood.

sources: PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - the treaty process. Adoption is by the relevant IMO organ or by a diplomatic conference. A State may express consent by signature alone where the treaty so provides; most multilateral treaties instead allow signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, where signature does not bind and the State must subsequently deposit a formal instrument with the depositary. The practice originated when communications were slow, protecting representatives from exceeding their authority, and States now use it to allow time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements. It cites Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Article 14(2) for acceptance and approval and Article 15 for accession.

PRIMARY (via MIW verification record QP2602/Q7): IMO conventions page - entry into force and amendment. A convention becomes binding only after governments formally accept it. Early conventions typically required acceptance by two-thirds of contracting States, which sometimes meant more acceptances were needed for entry into force than for amendments. Conventions of an important technical nature generally set higher requirements involving both a number of States and a percentage of world merchant fleet gross tonnage. The tacit acceptance procedure was devised to accelerate amendment: an amendment is deemed to have been accepted unless objections are received before a deadline. Amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances under the explicit procedure and none entered into force.

blocks.h: 1. Adoption is not entry into force

blocks.p: A convention is adopted either by the competent IMO organ - the Assembly, MSC, MEPC or Legal Committee - or by a diplomatic conference. Adoption settles the text and does no more: it binds no State, and an adopted convention may never enter into force at all. The text is then opened for signature and deposited with the Secretary-General of IMO as depositary.

blocks.h: 2. How a State expresses consent to be bound

blocks.p: Between adoption and entry into force sits the step that actually matters: each State must express its consent to be bound, by one of three routes -

ul: signature alone, where the treaty so provides or the negotiating States so agreed;
signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval, which is the normal course for multilateral conventions;
accession, where the State did not sign within the signature period.

blocks.p: In the second and third cases the State is bound only on depositing a formal instrument with the depositary, who records it, counts it towards the entry into force condition, and notifies all other States.

blocks.h: 3. The two terms the question names

blocks.p: (ii) Signature subject to ratification, acceptance or approval. The State signs, but the signature does not bind it; it indicates an intention to proceed. The State becomes a party only on later depositing an instrument of ratification. Its modern purpose is to give the State time to enact the necessary domestic legislation and satisfy constitutional requirements before committing internationally. Acceptance and approval are the same act under less formal names, used where a constitution does not demand the fuller procedure: VCLT Article 14(2) provides that consent is expressed by acceptance or approval under conditions similar to those which apply to ratification. In legal effect the three are identical.

(i) Accession. The means by which a State becomes party to a treaty it did not sign - because the signature period has closed, or because it was not a negotiating State. It is a single step: no prior signature, simply deposit of an instrument of accession, permitted by VCLT Article 15 where the treaty so provides. Once deposited it has exactly the same legal effect as ratification. The difference is the route, not the destination.

blocks.h: 4. The entry into force provision, and why it matters

blocks.p: Every convention contains a final clause fixing entry into force, normally a threshold of acceptances plus a waiting period. Its importance is fourfold:

ul: it prevents an instrument binding a handful of States while the rest operate to another standard, which would distort competition;
it fixes a certain date from which obligations, surveys and certificates run, so Administrations, recognised organisations, owners and yards all work to one deadline;
it provides the interval in which flag States legislate, class develops rules, and industry builds or retrofits;
it gives legitimacy - a convention in force across most world tonnage can be enforced through port State control against ships of non-parties, which is what makes no more favourable treatment work.

blocks.h: 5. Conventions of an important technical nature

blocks.p: For a convention of important technical nature - one dictating construction, equipment or operation - States observe a stiffer double condition: a number of States and a percentage of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping. A count of States alone could be satisfied by many small registries while the major fleets stayed outside, leaving a convention in force on paper and irrelevant at sea.

ul: SOLAS 1974 - adopted 1 November 1974, requiring not less than 25 States whose combined merchant fleets constitute not less than 50 per cent of the gross tonnage of the world's merchant shipping; in force 25 May 1980.
The 1978 MARPOL Protocol - in force twelve months after not less than fifteen States constituting not less than fifty per cent of world merchant shipping gross tonnage had become Parties.

blocks.p: Older conventions typically required two-thirds of contracting States, which occasionally meant more acceptances were needed to bring an instrument into force than to amend it.

blocks.h: 6. Keeping the convention current once in force

blocks.p: A technical convention is worthless if it cannot keep pace, and explicit acceptance failed on exactly that point: amendments to the 1960 SOLAS Convention adopted between 1966 and 1973 never received enough acceptances and none entered into force.

IMO's answer was the tacit acceptance procedure, used in SOLAS 1974, MARPOL and the collision regulations. It reverses the default: an amendment to the technical annexes is deemed accepted on a specified date unless objections are received beforehand from an agreed number of Parties. For SOLAS 1974 an amendment is deemed accepted at the end of two years from communication to Contracting Governments, unless objected to by more than one-third of Contracting Governments, or by Governments whose combined fleets are not less than 50 per cent of world gross merchant tonnage. Amendments now enter into force typically within 18 to 24 months.

The sequence can be seen running at this very sitting. Under MARPOL article 16(2)(a) the Secretary-General circulated the draft revised Annex VI on 11 April 2025 for consideration with a view to adoption at an extraordinary session under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d). Circulated, therefore, but not yet adopted - see Q8. Finally, once in force internationally each flag State must still give the instrument domestic effect, in India through the Merchant Shipping Act and the rules made under it, and it is that domestic instrument which is enforced against the ship.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem prints no limbs but contains four separate demands and then names two terms. The route answers them in the order asked and gives the two named terms a heading of their own, because the examiner has singled them out and an answer that defines them in passing inside a general narrative will not be credited for them. Step 6 is the pay-off: a candidate who can name tacit acceptance and say why explicit acceptance failed has shown he understands the machinery rather than memorised it.

blocks.h: Four words that are not synonyms

blocks.p: Adoption settles the text. Signature may or may not bind, depending on what the treaty says. Ratification, acceptance, approval or accession is the act that binds the State, and it binds on deposit, not on decision at home. Entry into force is when the instrument starts to operate, for those States and thereafter for later parties. Candidates use all four as though they meant the same thing, and the whole question is built on their not meaning the same thing.

blocks.h: The same problem exists in domestic law

blocks.p: This is worth noticing because this paper tests it twice. An Indian Act is passed, then receives assent, then commences on a date appointed by notification - and it is not law until it commences. That is structurally the same three-stage problem as adoption, ratification and entry into force. Q5 of this paper turns on it: the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 received assent in August 2025 and did not commence until March 2026. Revising Q5, Q7 and Q8 together is far more efficient than revising them apart, because they are one idea in three settings.

blocks.h: Why tonnage and not just a headcount

blocks.p: The double condition looks like bureaucratic detail and is in fact the most commercially significant sentence in the answer. A safety convention that binds fifty small registries and none of the major fleets creates a competitive distortion rather than a safety improvement: compliant ships carry the cost and non-compliant ships take the trade. Requiring a percentage of world gross tonnage ensures the instrument binds the fleet that actually carries the cargo, which is what then makes port State control and no more favourable treatment effective against the remainder.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Saying a convention applies once IMO adopts it. Adoption binds nobody.
Treating accession as a lesser status. Once deposited it has identical effect to ratification.
Saying ratification is deposit with IMO of a signed convention. It is deposit of a separate formal instrument.
Giving the entry into force condition as a number of States only, and omitting the tonnage percentage, on a question that expressly asks about conventions of important technical nature.
Describing tacit acceptance as automatic amendment. It is deemed acceptance in the absence of objection by a specified proportion.
Stopping at entry into force and never mentioning that the flag State must still give domestic effect - which is what actually binds the ship.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'State the provision and its importance' - two demands. Describing the provision without saying why it matters loses half of them.
'For a convention of important technical nature' - this signals the double condition of States plus tonnage. It is the single most specific thing the question asks for.

'Explain the terms (i) Accession (ii) Signature subject to Ratification, acceptance or approval' - two terms, expressly numbered. Answer them as such, and contrast them: one is a single step, the other is two.
The printed comma in 'technical nature state, the general rules' is on the paper. It joins two clauses; do not read it as a new demand.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Hold the spine as five words in order: ADOPT - SIGN - RATIFY - IN FORCE - AMEND. Then hang the numbers on it: SOLAS 1974 needed 25 States and 50% and took from 1974 to 1980; the 1978 MARPOL Protocol needed 15 States and 50% plus twelve months; tacit acceptance for SOLAS runs two years, defeated by one-third of Governments or 50% of tonnage. And remember the two named terms as a contrast: accession is one step, signature-subject-to-ratification is two.

blocks.h: Regulation and source map

ul: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 14(2) acceptance and approval; Article 15 accession.
SOLAS 1974 - entry into force condition (25 States, 50% world tonnage) and the tacit acceptance amendment procedure.
MARPOL - Article 15 entry into force; Article 16 amendments, with 16(2)(a) circulation and 16(2)(b), (c), (d) adoption; 1978 Protocol (15 States, 50%).
IMO Convention, Article 38(e) - the Organization's depositary and convention functions.
IMO Circular Letter No.5005, 11 April 2025 - a live worked example of the article 16(2)(a) circulation step. See Q8.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency

blocks.p: The treaty-making machinery is the most stable material in this paper: it has not changed materially since tacit acceptance was introduced, so nothing here is sitting-relative and no regression from the February 2026 donor was needed. The limitation is one of sourcing rather than currency. MIW holds no licensed copy of SOLAS, so the SOLAS entry into force and amendment provisions are cited from the IMO's own explanatory material and from convention summaries, by name and effect, rather than asserted with article numbers that could not be confirmed. The Vienna Convention was not read directly; Articles 14(2) and 15 are cited as quoted on the IMO page. MARPOL article 16(2) is the exception: its allocation of circulation to 16(2)(a) and adoption to 16(2)(b), (c) and (d) is quoted in Circular Letter No.5005, which was read in full for Q8, and is therefore primary here.

questions.understand_first: The point of this question is that a convention passes through several distinct stages, and at every stage it is not yet law for your ship. Adoption fixes the words. Signature usually promises nothing. Ratification or accession binds the State, and only when the instrument is physically deposited. Entry into force starts the obligations running. And even then, what is actually enforced against the ship in an Indian port is the domestic legislation giving effect to the convention. A Chief Engineer who can place an instrument on that ladder can answer 'does this apply to me?' - which is what the question is really about, and which Q8 of this same paper asks in a live case.

Regulation 32: two functional requirements - continuous improvement of the ship's GHG fuel intensity under regulation 35, and GHG emissions pricing contributions for excess emissions and rewards for the uptake of ZNZs under regulations 36 and 39. Regulation 33: after the end of calendar year 2028 and each year thereafter, the ship calculates its attained annual GFI over the 12-month period 1 January to 31 December.

PRIMARY: draft MARPOL Annex VI regulation 35 (target annual GFI), read in the draft text. The target is expressed as GFI(T) = (1 - Z(T)/100) x GFI(2008), where GFI(2008) is 93.3 gCO2eq/MJ (well-to-wake), 'representing the average GFI of international shipping in year 2008'. Table 4 gives the annual GFI reduction factors as two tiers, a Base target and a Direct compliance target: 2028 4.0% / 17.0%; 2029 6.0% / 19.0%; 2030 8.0% / 21.0%; 2031 12.4% / 25.4%; 2032 16.8% / 29.8%; 2033 21.2% / 34.2%; 2034 25.6% / 38.6%; 2035 30.0% / 43.0%. Paragraph 3 requires the Committee, by 1 January 2032, to determine the Z factors for 2036 to 2040, and provides that the 2040 Z factor for the Base target shall be set at 65%.

PRIMARY: draft MARPOL Annex VI regulation 36 (annual GFI compliance approaches), read in the draft text. The GFI compliance balance in tonnes of CO2eq is (direct compliance target annual GFI - attained annual GFI) x total energy. A balance at or above zero puts the ship in direct compliance and earns surplus units. A deficit is split into a Tier 1 deficit (attained GFI at or below the base target but above the direct compliance target) and a Tier 2 deficit (attained GFI above the base target). A Tier 1 deficit must be balanced by remedial units bought as GHG emissions pricing contributions to the IMO Net-Zero Fund; a Tier 2 deficit may be balanced by surplus units transferred from other ships, surplus units banked from previous periods, or Tier 2 remedial units. Paragraphs 8 and 9: for the reporting periods 2028 to 2030 the initial price of a Tier 1 remedial unit is US$100 per tonne of CO2eq and of a Tier 2 remedial unit US$380 per tonne of CO2eq, both on a well-to-wake basis; by 1 January 2028 the Committee is to determine the mechanism for reviewing prices from 2031. Paragraphs 11 to 15: surplus units may be transferred to another ship, banked, or voluntarily cancelled as a mitigation contribution, are used once, are automatically banked if unassigned, and have a validity of two calendar years after the year of issuance.

PRIMARY: draft MARPOL Annex VI regulations 39, 40, 41 and 44, read in the draft text. blocks.h: 1. What the revised strategy is, and what it is not

blocks.p: The 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships was adopted by resolution MEPC.377(80) on 7 July 2023 at MEPC 80, replacing the Initial Strategy of 2018. Its vision commits the Organization to reducing GHG emissions from international shipping and phasing them out as soon as possible, while promoting a just and equitable transition.

What it is must be stated precisely, because the second half of the question depends on it. The Strategy is an adopted policy resolution. It states intent, ambition and candidate measures. It is not mandatory law and binds no ship. Obligation arises only when a measure is written into MARPOL Annex VI and that amendment is adopted and enters into force. That gap between policy and law is precisely what the new Chapter V was drafted to close.

blocks.h: 2. The four levels of ambition

ol: Carbon intensity of the ship to decline - further improvement of the energy efficiency requirements for new ships;
carbon intensity of international shipping to decline - reduce CO2 emissions per transport work, as an average across international shipping, by at least 40% by 2030, compared to 2008;
uptake of zero or near-zero GHG technologies, fuels and/or energy sources to increase - to at least 5%, striving for 10%, of the energy used by international shipping by 2030;
GHG emissions to reach net zero - peak as soon as possible and reach net-zero by or around, i.e. close to, 2050, taking account of different national circumstances.

blocks.p: The ambitions are assessed well-to-wake, under the life cycle guidelines, so emissions cannot be moved off the ship and into the fuel production chain and counted as a saving.

blocks.h: 3. The indicative checkpoints and the guiding principles

blocks.p: Two indicative checkpoints are added. Unlike the ambitions, they are expressed in total annual GHG emissions: reduce them by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, and by at least 70%, striving for 80%, by 2040, both against 2008.

The guiding principles include non-discrimination and no more favourable treatment as enshrined in MARPOL; common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in the light of different national circumstances; and consideration of impacts on States, particularly LDCs and SIDS. Holding a uniform global measure and differentiated burden together is the central difficulty of the whole exercise.

blocks.h: 4. The basket of measures, and why Annex VI must be amended

blocks.p: Short-term measures are already mandatory under Annex VI - EEXI, the CII under regulation 28, and the SEEMP. For the mid-term the Strategy identifies a basket of two complementary elements: a technical element, a goal-based marine fuel standard phasing down the GHG intensity of the fuel used; and an economic element, a maritime GHG emissions pricing mechanism. They were designed to be delivered as one instrument - the standard sets the trajectory, the price makes falling short dearer than complying - and delivering them means amending MARPOL Annex VI, which is what the question refers to.

blocks.h: 5. The proposed new Chapter V - what the draft actually provides

blocks.p: That instrument is the IMO Net-Zero Framework, drafted as a new Chapter 5 of MARPOL Annex VI, 'Regulations on the IMO Net-Zero Framework', regulations 30 to 44. As drafted it would:

ul: apply to all ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, excluding ships trading solely within their own flag State's waters, ships not mechanically propelled, platforms and drilling rigs (reg 30);
require each ship, after the end of calendar year 2028 and annually thereafter, to calculate an attained annual GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) in gCO2eq/MJ on a well-to-wake basis (reg 33);

set a target annual GFI in two tiers - a Base target and a stricter Direct compliance target - as a percentage reduction from a 2008 reference value of 93.3 gCO2eq/MJ: 4.0% and 17.0% in 2028, 8.0% and 21.0% in 2030, rising to 30.0% and 43.0% by 2035 (reg 35);
require a ship in deficit to buy remedial units by making GHG emissions pricing contributions, priced for 2028 to 2030 at US$100 per tonne CO2eq (Tier 1) and US$380 (Tier 2) (reg 36);

allow a ship beating the Direct compliance target to earn surplus units, which may be transferred to another ship, banked, or voluntarily cancelled, and which are valid for two calendar years (reg 36);
reward zero or near-zero (ZNZ) technologies, fuels and energy sources - those at not more than 19.0 gCO2eq/MJ, tightening to 14.0 from 1 January 2035 (reg 39);

channel contributions into an IMO Net-Zero Fund which rewards ZNZ uptake and supports innovation, capacity building and technology transfer in developing countries, governed by a board with assured representation of SIDS and LDCs (regs 40 and 41);
require a review every five years, which may amend the reduction factors and the ZNZ thresholds and may consider extending the chapter to ships of 400 gross tonnage and above (reg 44).

blocks.h: 6. Where the amendments stood at this sitting

blocks.p: The stem says the amendments are being considered, and that is exactly right. MEPC 83, which met from 7 to 11 April 2025, considered and approved the draft amendments, including the Net-Zero Framework as new Chapter 5. On 11 April 2025 the Secretary-General transmitted the draft revised consolidated Annex VI to all Parties by Circular Letter No.5005, expressly in accordance with article 16(2)(a) of MARPOL, for consideration with a view to adoption at a second extraordinary session of the Committee, MEPC/ES.2, convened for 14 to 17 October 2025, under article 16(2)(b), (c) and (d).

So at the date of this examination the position was: the Framework was approved and formally circulated, but not yet adopted and not in force. The adoption session had not yet been held. If the amendments were adopted as scheduled and accepted under the tacit acceptance procedure, entry into force would follow after the stated period, with the first GFI reporting period being calendar year 2028.

The accurate summary is therefore in three parts: the Strategy is adopted policy; the short-term measures are in force; and the mid-term measures are an approved and circulated draft awaiting an adoption session. Every figure in Chapter V above is precise, and every one of them is provisional until adoption.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: The stem contains two demands and prints no limbs, so the standing risk is an undifferentiated essay on decarbonisation. Steps 1 to 3 discharge the Strategy, step 4 is the hinge that explains why a Chapter V is needed at all, and steps 5 to 6 discharge the amendments. Step 6 is what turns a good answer into a full-marks one, because the examiner's own words - amendments being considered - show that he is testing status, not enthusiasm.

blocks.h: Read the stem as a date stamp

blocks.p: Amendments being considered under MARPOL Annex VI, including the inclusion of new Chapter-V is not loose drafting. In August 2025 it was a precise description: the text had been approved at MEPC 83 in April and circulated under article 16(2)(a), and the session convened to adopt it was still four months away. An answer that describes the Framework as being in force contradicts the question itself. An answer that gives the approval and the scheduled adoption is answering the question that was asked.

blocks.h: Strategy, approval, circulation, adoption, entry into force

blocks.p: This question is the live worked example of the machinery examined in Q7 of this same paper, and the two are best revised together. The sequence is: a strategy states intent; a committee approves a draft text; the Secretary-General circulates it to Parties under article 16(2)(a), which is the step that starts the clock; a session adopts it, which is what makes it an amendment; and it then enters into force, ordinarily by tacit acceptance. At this sitting the Net-Zero Framework had completed approval and circulation and had reached, but not passed, adoption. Being able to name which of those five stages an instrument has reached is worth more marks than any amount of detail about fuels.

blocks.h: Why the numbers are precise and provisional at the same time

blocks.p: The figures in step 5 are quoted from the draft regulations as circulated, so they are exact rather than approximate - the reduction factors sit in a table in draft regulation 35, and the two unit prices in draft regulation 36. But a draft is only a proposal until a session adopts it. The right way to write them in an examination is with the qualification attached: as drafted, the draft would require. That costs four words and protects the whole answer.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Describing the Net-Zero Framework as adopted, in force, or as binding law. At this sitting it was an approved and circulated draft.
Treating the 2023 Strategy as mandatory. It is a policy resolution and binds no ship.
Mixing the levels of ambition with the indicative checkpoints - carbon intensity and fuel uptake against total annual emissions.
Dropping the striving for figures, which are part of the adopted wording.
Omitting the 2008 baseline, without which every percentage is meaningless.
Forgetting the well-to-wake basis, which is what stops emissions being exported upstream into fuel production.
Confusing GFI with CII. GFI is the GHG intensity of the fuel, in gCO2eq/MJ; CII is the operational carbon intensity of the ship.
Quoting the 2018 Initial Strategy targets. The question says revised.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Revised' GHG strategy - the 2023 Strategy, resolution MEPC.377(80). A candidate quoting the 2018 figures has answered a different instrument.
'Amendments being considered' - the status is part of the question, not background to it.

'To achieve the decarbonisation goal and transition to a Net Zero future' invites rhetoric. The marks are in the resolution number, the percentages, the baseline, the regulation numbers and the status.

blocks.h: Likely oral follow-up

ul: Is the Net-Zero Framework law? What still has to happen before it is?
What is the difference between GFI and CII?
Why well-to-wake rather than tank-to-wake?
Your ship is 4,800 GT. Would the draft Chapter V apply to her?
What is a surplus unit, and what are the three things you may do with one?
What does article 16(2)(a) of MARPOL require, and why does it matter here?

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Hold the Strategy as 4 ambitions, 2 checkpoints, 1 baseline year, remembering that ambitions measure intensity and fuel while checkpoints measure total emissions. Hold the numbers in pairs: 40 by 2030; 5 striving 10 by 2030; 20 striving 30 by 2030, 70 striving 80 by 2040. Hold Chapter V as a standard plus a price: GFI down from 93.3, shortfall bought at 100 or 380, ZNZ at 19. And hold the status in four words: approved, circulated, awaiting adoption.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and currency - what happened after this sitting

blocks.p: The Strategy content is primary and stable, read in resolution MEPC.377(80). The status finding is primary and unusually strong: it rests on Circular Letter No.5005 itself, which is the article 16(2)(a) circulation, and the numeric content of Chapter V is read in the draft regulations annexed to it rather than taken from a summary. What remains genuinely open is the fate of the draft, which was undecided at the sitting and could not have been known.

Current study note - events after the examination. A candidate revising this today must know what happened next, and must keep it strictly separate from the answer above. The extraordinary session MEPC/ES.2 did meet on 14 to 17 October 2025, could not reach consensus, and was adjourned to be reconvened in twelve months' time without adopting the amendments. The Framework therefore remained approved but unadopted well beyond this sitting. None of that belongs in an answer to this August 2025 paper, where the adoption session was still in the future: writing it in would describe as history something that had not yet happened. It is stated here because the same stem was set again in February 2026, when the adjournment was part of the correct answer - see the cross-link to that paper.

blocks.h: 1. a) The zones, and what the coastal State holds in each

blocks.p: UNCLOS measures the zones from the baselines, and the coastal State's authority thins progressively seaward - from full sovereignty, to defined functional rights, to none at all.

ul: Internal waters - landward of the baselines. Full sovereignty, and no right of innocent passage.
Territorial sea, up to 12 n.m. - sovereignty, extending to the airspace above and the seabed and subsoil below, subject to innocent passage.
Contiguous zone, to 24 n.m. - not sovereignty but control, to prevent and punish infringement of customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary laws.
Exclusive Economic Zone, to 200 n.m. - sovereign rights, which is not the same as sovereignty.
Continental shelf - sovereign rights over the seabed and subsoil, existing independently of occupation or proclamation.
High seas - no State may validly claim sovereignty; the high seas freedoms apply.

blocks.h: 2. What the coastal State may actually do

ul: Territorial sea - full prescriptive and enforcement jurisdiction; its criminal and civil law applies. It may legislate on navigation, cables, fishing, pollution and customs, but must not hamper innocent passage, which ceases to be innocent on acts prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal State.
Contiguous zone - powers confined to those four subjects, and only to prevent or punish.

EEZ - Article 56 gives sovereign rights for exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing the natural resources, living and non-living, together with jurisdiction over artificial islands and installations, marine scientific research and protection of the marine environment. Article 73 permits boarding, inspection and arrest for fisheries offences.
The limit is the whole point: outside those purposes the coastal State has no general jurisdiction in the EEZ. It is not territory.

blocks.h: 3. The flag State - nationality, freedoms and exclusive jurisdiction

ul: Article 91 - each State fixes the conditions for granting its nationality and for registration; a genuine link must exist between State and ship.
Article 92 - a ship sails under one flag only and is subject to the flag State's exclusive jurisdiction on the high seas.

Article 94 - the flag State must effectively exercise jurisdiction and control in administrative, technical and social matters - construction, equipment, seaworthiness, manning, labour conditions and training - and must hold an inquiry into serious casualties.

Article 58 - in the EEZ all States retain the freedoms of navigation and overflight, and Articles 88 to 115, which include Article 92, apply so far as they are not incompatible with the EEZ regime. The flag State's authority therefore travels with the ship into the EEZ.

blocks.h: 4. How the two are reconciled - due regard

blocks.p: UNCLOS resolves the overlap by a reciprocal standard rather than a hierarchy. The coastal State exercises its EEZ rights with due regard to the rights and duties of other States; other States exercise their freedoms with due regard to the rights and duties of the coastal State and comply with its laws made in conformity with the Convention. Where the Convention attributes no right to either, the conflict is resolved on the basis of equity and all relevant circumstances. And across every zone, Article 98 obliges every master to render assistance to any person found in danger of being lost at sea.

blocks.h: 5. b) The missing cadet - which law applies

blocks.p: The tempting answer is that Indian law applies because the ship was in India's EEZ. That is wrong. The EEZ is not Indian territory; India's authority there is functional - resources, installations, research, the marine environment - and a person missing from a ship engages none of it. Because Article 58 carries Article 92 into the EEZ, matters internal to the ship remain under the exclusive jurisdiction of the flag State. The determining question is therefore whose flag the vessel flies, and the paper does not say.

ul: Indian-flagged - Indian law applies in full, through the flag. Under the Merchant Shipping Act 1958: s.358, loss of life by reason of a casualty on board is a shipping casualty, and the master must give immediate notice to the officer appointed by the Central Government; s.359, that officer reports in writing to the Central Government and may hold a preliminary inquiry; s.452, the proper officer inquires into the cause of death, endorses the official log book as to whether the stated cause is in his opinion true, and if death appears to have been caused by violence or other improper means reports to the Director-General. Indian criminal law reaches the ship through section 1(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 - any offence committed on a ship registered in India wherever it may be.

Foreign-flagged - the flag State's law governs the investigation and any prosecution, and its Administration conducts the casualty investigation. India acts as coastal State and, decisively, as the State responsible for search and rescue within its search and rescue region - a duty owed regardless of flag under Article 98 and the SAR Convention. India may also be a substantially interested State if the cadet was an Indian national.

blocks.h: 6. The actions to be taken

ol: Immediate. Raise the man overboard alarm and mark the position; muster and account for every person on board to establish who is missing and when last seen, because the search datum has to be reconstructed. Commence a search, return along the track, post lookouts, and broadcast to the MRCC and to ships in the vicinity.
Preserve. Secure the cabin and the last known location; preserve CCTV, gangway and access records, rest-hour records and personal effects; take statements early; make full official log book entries.
Notify. Owner and manager, the DPA, the flag State, the coordinating coastal State authority, the P&I club, the manning agent, and - through the company - the next of kin.

Report and investigate. Loss of life makes this a very serious marine casualty, so a safety investigation follows under the Casualty Investigation Code alongside the flag State's inquiry; for an Indian ship the s.358 notice and the s.359 report apply, with the s.452 inquiry into cause of death on arrival.

Company review and welfare. Treat it under the ISM Code as an accident and a non-conformity - safety of access, work overside, lifebuoy provision, fatigue, and bullying, harassment or isolation all examined honestly - and discharge the MLC 2006 obligations on repatriation of remains, compensation for death and support to dependants, while supporting the remaining crew.

blocks.h: Why this structure scores

blocks.p: Limb (a) asks about both States and most answers describe only the coastal one. Splitting the limb into coastal State, flag State and the due-regard reconciliation guarantees that the flag half is present, and it sets up limb (b), which cannot be answered without it. Limb (b) is worth only 6 marks but it contains the single highest-value insight in the question, so it should be led with the jurisdictional point rather than with a list of actions.

blocks.h: Why the EEZ is the way it is

blocks.p: The EEZ was the great compromise of UNCLOS III. Coastal States - especially newly independent ones - wanted the fish and the oil off their coasts; maritime States wanted their ships and aircraft to keep moving. The zone gives each side what it actually needed: economic control to the coastal State and navigational freedom to everyone else. Understanding that bargain tells you at once what the coastal State can and cannot do, without memorising a list. If the issue is a resource, an installation, research or pollution, it is the coastal State's. If it is about the ship as a ship - her navigation, her crew, her internal affairs - it remains the flag State's.

blocks.h: Sovereignty, sovereign rights, jurisdiction - three different words

ul: Sovereignty - the full authority of a State over its territory. Internal waters and territorial sea.
Sovereign rights - exclusive rights for a defined purpose. The EEZ and the continental shelf. Exclusive, but purposive.
Jurisdiction - the power to prescribe and enforce law over specified subject matter, such as artificial islands or marine scientific research in the EEZ.

blocks.p: The question uses the phrase sovereign rights and jurisdictions deliberately, and an answer that treats the three as interchangeable has missed what is being tested.

blocks.h: Missing is not the same as dead

blocks.p: The scenario says the cadet goes missing, not that he was seen to fall or that a body was recovered, and the distinction has practical and legal consequences. Practically, the search datum must be reconstructed from the last confirmed sighting rather than from a known position, which is why the muster is the critical first step and why gangway records and CCTV matter so much. Legally, a presumption of death normally requires a formal process and takes time, which affects wages, the seafarer employment agreement, insurance and the family's ability to deal with the estate. A candidate who writes as though a death certificate follows automatically has misunderstood the situation the crew is actually in.

blocks.h: Common mistakes

ul: Assuming Indian law applies because the incident was in India's EEZ. The EEZ is not territory.
Forgetting to ask what flag the ship flies - the question does not say, and that omission is the test.
Describing only the coastal State's rights in limb (a) and ignoring the flag State.
Saying the coastal State has sovereignty in the EEZ, or that it has no rights there at all. Neither is right.
Citing the Indian Penal Code, which was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 on 1 July 2024 - more than a year before this sitting.
Treating search and rescue as depending on jurisdiction. It does not: Article 98 and the SAR Convention apply regardless of flag.
Jumping straight to actions in limb (b) without answering the question asked, which is which laws will apply.

blocks.h: Examiner traps

ul: 'Coastal state and Flag state' - both are named in the stem and both must be answered.
'In the Exclusive Economic zone of India' - written to invite the wrong answer.
'Which laws will apply' comes before 'what actions will be taken'. Answer them in that order or the analysis reads as an afterthought.
The printed phrase 'Explain your answer suitable explanations' is incomplete on the paper. It means give reasons; do not lose time over it.

blocks.h: Memory framework

blocks.p: Sail outward and watch authority thin: internal (all) - territorial 12 (all, but passage) - contiguous 24 (four subjects) - EEZ 200 (resources only) - shelf (seabed) - high seas (none). Then remember that the flag State's authority is constant across all of them, which is why limb (b) resolves as it does. For the incident: WHOSE FLAG, then SEARCH, SECURE, REPORT, INQUIRE, SUPPORT.

quick_revision.major_trap: Assuming that because the incident occurred in India's Exclusive Economic Zone, Indian law applies. The EEZ is not territory: India's rights there are functional and concern resources, artificial islands, research and the marine environment, none of which reaches a person missing from a ship. What happens on board follows the flag, and the paper deliberately does not say what that flag is. India's search and rescue responsibility is a separate duty and does apply regardless of flag. A second trap is citing the Indian Penal Code, which the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaced on 1 July 2024, more than a year before this paper was sat.

steps.title: a) The zones, and what the coastal State holds in each
points: internal waters - full sovereignty, no innocent passage
territorial sea up to 12 n.m. - sovereignty, subject to innocent passage

EEZ to 200 n.m. - sovereign rights over resources only

points: territorial sea - full prescriptive and enforcement jurisdiction
but must not hamper innocent passage
contiguous zone - customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary only
EEZ - exploring, exploiting, conserving, managing resources
plus artificial islands, marine scientific research, environment
Article 73 enforcement over fisheries; no general jurisdiction

points: Article 91 - grant of nationality, genuine link
Article 92 - exclusive jurisdiction over its ships
Article 94 - administrative, technical and social matters

questions.understand_first: The phrase in the Exclusive Economic Zone of India tempts everyone into the same error. The EEZ is not Indian territory. India holds only functional rights there - over resources, artificial islands, research and the marine environment - and nothing in that list covers a person going missing from a ship. What happens on board a ship is an internal matter of the ship, and internal matters follow the flag. So the first question is never 'where did it happen' but 'whose flag is she flying' - and only then does India's role become clear: search and rescue always, because that duty is owed to everyone, but investigation and prosecution only if she is Indian.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) sails outward: INTERNAL - TERRITORIAL - CONTIGUOUS - EEZ - SHELF - HIGH SEAS (1), rights thinning as you go (2), then the flag State's constant authority (3) and due regard where they meet (4). Limb (b): WHOSE FLAG (5), then SEARCH - SECURE - REPORT - INQUIRE - SUPPORT (6). Limits 12, 24, 200.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the UNCLOS zones and missing cadet question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The zones and what the coastal State holds in each. 2 What the coastal State may actually do. 3 The flag State - nationality, freedoms and exclusive jurisdiction. 4 Due regard. 5 The missing cadet - which law applies. 6 The actions to be taken.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 1 to 4 are the 10-mark limb, steps 5 and 6 the 6-mark limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the difference between sovereignty in the territorial sea and sovereign rights in the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: In the territorial sea the coastal State has full sovereignty, subject only to innocent passage, so its laws apply generally. In the EEZ it has only sovereign rights for a defined purpose - exploring, exploiting, conserving and managing natural resources - plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and the marine environment. It is functional authority, not territory.
retrieval_cards.why: This single distinction decides limb (b) and is the highest-value sentence in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the outer limits of the territorial sea, contiguous zone and EEZ.
retrieval_cards.answer: Territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles from the baselines; contiguous zone up to 24 nautical miles; exclusive economic zone up to 200 nautical miles.
retrieval_cards.why: Three numbers that anchor the whole of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does UNCLOS Article 92 provide, and does it help in the EEZ?
retrieval_cards.answer: That ships are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the flag State. It matters in the EEZ because Article 58 applies the high seas articles to the EEZ so far as they are not incompatible with the EEZ regime, so matters internal to the ship continue to follow the flag.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the chain of reasoning that takes you from a scenario set in the EEZ to the flag State's law.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A cadet goes missing in India's EEZ. Does Indian law automatically apply?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. The EEZ is not Indian territory and India's rights there do not extend to matters internal to the ship. If the ship is Indian-flagged, Indian law applies through the flag. If she is foreign-flagged, the flag State's law governs investigation and prosecution, though India retains search and rescue responsibility within its search and rescue region.
retrieval_cards.why: The question deliberately does not state the flag, and noticing that gap is what the examiner is testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian merchant shipping provisions bite if the ship is Indian-flagged and a person is lost?
retrieval_cards.answer: MSA 1958 section 358, under which loss of life by reason of a casualty on board is a shipping casualty and the master must give immediate notice; section 359, under which the officer reports to the Central Government and may hold a preliminary inquiry; and section 452, under which the proper officer inquires into the cause of death, endorses the official log book, and reports to the Director-General if death appears to have been caused by violence or other improper means.
retrieval_cards.why: Three named sections turn a general answer about procedure into a legal one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which Indian penal statute reaches an offence committed on board an Indian ship, and since when?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, section 1(5), which applies to any offence committed by any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be. It came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code 1860 - so it was already the law more than a year before this August 2025 sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the IPC was already a currency error at this sitting, and it is exactly the sort of superseded-instrument trap this series keeps producing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the master's immediate actions when a person is found missing at sea?
retrieval_cards.answer: Raise the man overboard alarm and mark the position, muster and account for every person on board to confirm who is missing and when last seen, commence a search and return towards the search datum, broadcast to the MRCC and to ships in the vicinity, and preserve the scene, CCTV and access records while the search continues.
retrieval_cards.why: Missing is not the same as seen to fall - accounting for all hands is what establishes the datum, and it is the step most often omitted.
